papers_seen.author: Richard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically effective family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Research across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings has expanded KD from simple logits matching into diverse transfer signals (features, attention, relational/contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation), and data regimes (full-data, few-shot, data-free, privacy‑constrained, federated). Empirical evidence shows KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when its design is matched to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; however, its success is conditional and benefits from integration with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD has been shown to work across modalities and tasks by transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure. It can also be combined with data augmentation, adversarial schemes, online or teacher-free training, and architecture-aware adaptations to meet deployment constraints. KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices about which teacher signals to transfer, alignment of inputs and architectures, student capacity, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. When used as part of a task-aware compression pipeline that addresses these issues, KD delivers substantial practical benefits for latency- and resource-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to compact student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels of supervision, support varied training protocols, and are commonly integrated with complementary compression primitives to satisfy latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Practical success depends on careful choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness and fairness; remaining challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors, and principled guidance for heterogeneous architectures and federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Preston
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — An Argument for Integrated, Context‑Aware Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically effective and widely adopted approach for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels — logits, intermediate features, attention, relational and contrastive signals — and follow varied training protocols (offline, online/self, multi‑teacher, data‑free, and privacy‑aware). Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and generative settings show KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute; however, practical deployment requires careful matching of distilled signals to student capacity, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture design. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone solution, and I offer concrete, research‑ and practice‑informed recommendations for how to apply KD robustly in deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Landry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Tool That Must Be Integrated for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and generative domains. Empirical evidence shows KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its effectiveness is strongly context dependent: it hinges on what signals are transferred, teacher and student capacity and alignment, availability and composition of data, and mitigation of robustness, fairness, and low‑frequency behavior issues. Therefore, KD should be treated as a first‑line, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation‑aware distillation with data strategies, projector or layer‑mapping modules, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to produce robust, deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Tool for Compression, Adaptation, Privacy, and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single compression recipe: it is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from one set of models to another. KD enables production of compact, fast models that retain much of a larger model's performance, and it can be adapted to address domain shift, limited or private data, modality-specific constraints, and even fairness or robustness objectives. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of model deployment pipelines across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and sequential tasks) and that careful selection among KD variants (logit, feature, ensemble, online, adversarial, data-free, teacher-free, and task-aware distillation) lets practitioners balance accuracy, latency, privacy, and fairness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, configurable family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger 'teacher' models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster 'student' models to meet latency, memory, energy, or privacy constraints. Modern KD extends far beyond simple logits matching: practitioners match intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals, or use contrastive and adversarial objectives; they apply online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data‑free protocols; and they combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is most effective when treated as a component within an integrated compression pipeline that is aligned to task objectives, teacher/student architectures, available data, and deployment constraints. Important limits remain — teacher–student capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, distribution shift, and scarce or private transfer data — which motivate task-aware design, data synthesis or privacy-preserving workflows, and careful evaluation prior to deployment.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature develops multi-level transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), multi‑teacher and online variants, data-aware and data‑free protocols, and integrations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and mapping between teacher and student are carefully managed; however, success is context-dependent and limited by optimization gaps, data scarcity, capacity mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher artifacts or biases. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression workflows tailored to deployment constraints such as latency, memory, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression methods form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, efficient student models. Over the past decade KD variants—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to representation-level matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data- or privacy-aware protocols—have been adapted to many tasks and modalities (vision, language, speech, multimodal, generative models, and federated settings). Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves most teacher performance while enabling large reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count; success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability, and optimization. Remaining challenges include principled theory for when and what to transfer, reliable distillation across heterogeneous architectures and non‑i.i.d. data, mitigation of bias and teacher errors, and robust data-free or privacy-preserving protocols.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining much of the teacher’s performance. The literature shows a diverse toolkit of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure, channel statistics, and contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free variants), and task-aware adaptations (layer mapping, projector modules, synthetic-data generation, and curriculum/annealing). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, multimodal tasks, and continual or federated settings demonstrates substantial efficiency gains but also highlights persistent challenges: teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatch, limited or unavailable training data, propagation of teacher biases or errors, distribution shift, and difficulties transferring rare or low-frequency behaviors. Practical success typically requires matching the distillation signal to task and student capacity and integrating KD with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core method for producing compact, efficient models from large deep networks across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD delivers substantial inference and memory savings while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, enabling deployment in latency-, power-, and privacy-constrained settings. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections (biases, distributional blind spots) and faces practical constraints (data mismatch, teacher–student capacity gaps, limited-data regimes). Effective use of KD therefore requires matching objectives, data strategies, and architectures to deployment goals and complementing distillation with pruning, quantization, or privacy-aware protocols when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Necessary but Not Sufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible framework for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings. KD preserves much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its effectiveness depends on choices about what is distilled, how teacher and student are aligned, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression techniques. Practical success therefore requires integrating KD with task-aware engineering—data strategies, multi-objective compression (pruning/quantization/architecture search), teacher/student co-design, and privacy-aware protocols—to avoid known failure modes and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while enabling adaptation across tasks, domains, and modalities. When combined with representation-level objectives, careful teacher engineering, pre-training of compact architectures, and input-side interventions (e.g., augmentation or data synthesis), KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss and can enable deployment under tight compute, latency, or privacy constraints. At the same time, KD is not a single recipe: success depends on optimization choices, teacher–student alignment, and dataset properties, which motivates tailored distillation objectives, data strategies, and evaluation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods used to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD techniques extend from soft-logit matching to representation- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and federated protocols, and data-free or synthetic-data alternatives. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and inference cost; however, its effectiveness is context dependent and typically benefits from integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task- or data-aware design. Key open challenges include principled selection of distillation targets, reliable distillation under limited or mismatched data, mitigation of transferred biases and rare-case degradation, and theoretical understanding of when and why particular KD strategies succeed.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted framework for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative modeling, and multimodal tasks, KD methods trade off accuracy, latency, and resource use by transferring different forms of information (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, or synthesized training examples). Empirical work shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve generalization and deployment feasibility, but KD has practical limits tied to teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, bias transfer, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment mixes careful choice of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, multi-teacher or confidence-weighting schemes, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Butler
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When applied thoughtfully — choosing appropriate distillation targets, aligning teacher and student capacity, selecting or synthesizing data, and combining KD with complementary compression methods — KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. However, KD is context dependent: it has known failure modes (teacher–student capacity gaps, propagated biases, loss of rare or long‑tail behaviors, and domain shift) that require targeted remedies and integration with other compression primitives and data strategies. I argue KD should be treated as the configurable core of any compression pipeline, not a stand‑alone panacea, and I outline practical design principles and open problems to guide robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Carson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods are diverse—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—and are most effective when integrated with complementary compression tools and deployment-aware data and optimization strategies. Empirical work shows KD routinely delivers substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but important limitations remain around teacher imperfection, teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, privacy, and reliable preservation of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Clayton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–performance tradeoffs, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate data. For robust production use, KD should be treated as a configurable, task‑aware core element embedded in integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-level objectives, projector or layer‑mapping modules, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning and quantization. Careful engineering is required to avoid propagating teacher errors or biases and to preserve rare or low‑frequency behaviors under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. A diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational structure, and decision-boundary or synthetic-data signals), training protocols (single/multi-teacher, online/self-distillation, task- and layer-aware schedules), and architecture-aware adaptations (projectors, layer mapping, and combinations with pruning/quantization/NAS) has been developed. Empirically, properly designed distillation pipelines recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks, and can be combined with complementary compression methods to meet device and domain requirements. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps, teacher–student capacity mismatch, distribution shift and data scarcity (including privacy- and data-free regimes), and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Estrada
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods range from matching output probabilities to aligning internal representations, relational structures, or synthesized training data, and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware adaptations. Practical success is conditional on choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and mitigations for bias and rare-case degradation; integrating KD into broader, task-aware compression pipelines is the prevailing best practice.

papers_seen.author: Bender
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. A rich set of methods—ranging from logits/soft-target supervision to intermediate-feature matching, contrastive and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and is routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture/parameter adaptations). Empirical and conceptual work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, signal choice, data availability or synthesis strategy, and careful integration with other compression tools. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all solution.

papers_seen.author: Duarte
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (logits, features, relations) and in varied data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free), and they are most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task-aware choices about what to transfer. While KD often preserves much of teacher performance, its success is context-dependent: it relies on teacher quality, student capacity, suitable data or synthetic-data protocols, and explicit strategies to protect rare outputs and fairness under distribution shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution, and I provide actionable guidance and open problems to prioritize in research and practice.

papers_seen.author: Mccormick
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When designed with attention to which signals to transfer, student capacity and architecture, and distillation-data strategies, and when combined with complementary compression primitives, KD routinely yields favorable tradeoffs between efficiency and performance across modalities. However, KD is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on mitigating failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded rare‑token behavior, teacher–student mismatch, and distributional shift. Treating KD as a configurable, task‑aware element of integrated compression pipelines — rather than a turnkey replacement for other techniques — produces the most reproducible deployments and points to principled research directions for robust, privacy‑aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for producing smaller, faster, and deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. Research has expanded KD beyond logits-only supervision into a rich set of objectives (feature and representation matching, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial/data-free schemes, and self-distillation), and into diverse data regimes from full-data to data-free, few-shot, federated, and privacy-constrained workflows. KD is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, low-precision numerics) and with teacher-aware or student-aware design choices; its empirical success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data strategies. Remaining challenges include handling architecture and distributional mismatch, avoiding propagation of teacher errors and biases (especially on low-frequency phenomena), providing privacy and robustness guarantees, and automating teacher–student co-design for task-specific outputs.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Summers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models or ensembles into smaller, deployable student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while retaining much of task performance. Modern KD methods span soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence indicates KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and suitable data strategies are aligned, but its success is context-dependent and requires task-aware design to mitigate limits related to teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, widely used toolbox to transfer behavior and representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, resource-efficient students. The approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or generated samples), whether original training data are available, and whether the objective emphasizes efficiency, privacy, robustness, or interpretability. Across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks, carefully designed distillation objectives and training pipelines—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search—produce compact models that approach teacher performance under deployment constraints. Key practical challenges are capacity and optimization mismatch between teacher and student, data- and privacy-limited settings, distribution shift and low-frequency phenomena, and the risk of transferring undesirable teacher traits; promising responses include task-aware filtering of teacher signals, multi-layer mapping strategies, data-free sample synthesis, and privacy-preserving noise mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component of a broader compression pipeline, KD can deliver substantial gains in latency, memory, and often accuracy while enabling deployment in resource- and privacy-constrained settings. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, signal selection, and complementary compression methods. Responsible application requires explicit mitigation of failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and bias transfer, and integration with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, or data‑free methods when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Schmidt
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. A large and consistent body of work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities when the distilled signals, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen carefully. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness is context-dependent: it is bounded by data availability, teacher quality, capacity mismatch, and risks of transferring undesirable behaviors, so it is best applied as part of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD should be treated as the central, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines—paired with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and task‑aware engineering—because its success depends on teacher/student alignment, distilled signals, data regimes, and explicit mitigation of failure modes. KD rarely suffices on its own for reliable, deployment‑grade compression.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for training smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks, KD methods transfer predictive and representational signals (soft logits, internal features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and operate under a range of training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches). Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, distillation signals, and data strategy are chosen carefully. Practical deployment typically treats KD as a core, configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also includes pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data-side strategies. Open challenges include principled theory of transferable signals, robust distillation under data scarcity and heterogeneity, privacy-aware or data-free methods, and preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile framework that enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component—combining logits, intermediate-feature matching, contrastive objectives, data augmentation, and privacy-aware techniques—distillation supports deployment across modalities and constrained devices. However, KD is not automatic: it propagates some teacher errors, can lose low-frequency or structured information, and requires careful design choices (teacher selection, objective weighting, data strategy). A principled practice that matches the distillation objective to the task, augments or tailors distillation data, and applies privacy- or domain-aware protocols yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, pragmatic family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regimes, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Reyes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings, practitioners use KD to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Modern distillation extends beyond matching output probabilities to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware choices, pruning, quantization, curriculum or data strategies, and safeguards for fairness and robustness. Remaining challenges include teacher–student capacity mismatch, distributional and low-frequency phenomena, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and principled automation of distillation design.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller students. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals, synthetic data) and in protocol (offline, online, self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, data-free variants). Empirical results across vision, language, generation, and graph domains demonstrate that distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is carefully designed and combined with complementary compression techniques; however, success depends on factors such as teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes including bias transfer and degraded performance on rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also uses pretraining, architecture-aware design, and safeguards for privacy and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: an Essential, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied with task-aware design, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. However, KD is context-dependent: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of bias, low-frequency/fine-grained behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Salinas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, diverse family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large or composite teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. The field has evolved from matching soft output probabilities to include feature- and layer-level imitation, attention and relational transfer, contrastive and adversarial objectives, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols, and online or multi-teacher schemes. KD is effective across modalities and tasks (vision, NLP, speech, graphs, and multimodal systems) and often forms part of a broader compression pipeline together with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD success depends on task-aware choices—teacher quality, student capacity, the distillation signal, and the data available—and several practical challenges remain, including distribution shift, data heterogeneity (especially in federated settings), low-frequency/rare-token behavior, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Robbins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has established itself as a primary mechanism for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning intermediate features and representations, and they are readily combined with quantization, pruning, ensembling, and domain-adaptation techniques. While KD frequently yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance degradation—and sometimes performance improvements—its success depends on careful method selection, teacher quality, data and sample selection, and complementary engineering such as layer alignment or teacher-student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Component for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, versatile approach for producing compact models from larger teachers, but its practical success is context-dependent. KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when combined with task-aware design, appropriate distillation signals, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: limitations such as teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, propagated biases, degraded rare-case behavior, and distribution-shift sensitivity mean it should be treated as a core element within integrated, deployment-aware compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a rich, task-sensitive toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to compact students. Practitioners move beyond simple logit matching to transfer internal representations, attention patterns, relational structure, and decision-boundary information, and they combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Empirical results across vision, language, generative models, and structured prediction show distilled students often recover much of teacher performance and can enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but distillation also has failure modes—teacher bias transfer, sensitivity to data availability, capacity mismatch, and degraded modeling of low-frequency phenomena—that require targeted mitigations and continued theoretical and empirical work.

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD routinely achieves strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities and tasks when its objectives, teacher–student design, data strategies, and complementary compression methods are chosen with deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution, and explicit safeguards against bias, robustness, and privacy failures. Best practice treats KD as a configurable building block embedded in an integrated compression pipeline tailored to the task and environment.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Myers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD offers a wide set of distillation signals and protocols that generalize across modalities and deployment scenarios, but its success is conditional on teacher and student design, data regime, and integration with complementary compression methods. For reliable, robust deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Reyes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Core of Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows that KD often preserves much of teacher performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count; however, its success is context dependent and it must be integrated with complementary compression, data, and safety strategies for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. The literature characterizes a wide taxonomy of distillation targets and protocols, documents strong empirical gains when KD is carefully configured, and emphasizes that KD is most reliable when integrated into hybrid compression pipelines that address teacher–student alignment, data regime, and deployment constraints. Known limitations include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and bias, difficulties under data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability under distribution shift; current best practice is task- and deployment-aware application of KD combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Conditional Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD succeeds by transferring rich forms of information — soft logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive structure, and even synthesized data — and by being combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not an automatic remedy: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and privacy constraints, and defenses against transferring teacher errors or low-frequency phenomena. Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component within a broader compression pipeline, and adopting practices such as layer- and task-aware objectives, multi-teacher confidence weighting, adversarial or decision-boundary sample generation, and data-aware synthesis or augmentation, yields the most reliable trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity. Remaining research directions include principled guidance for selecting which signals to transfer, robust privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical framework for producing compact models from larger teachers. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful treatment of bias, low-frequency phenomena, and domain shift. Best practice treats KD as a central component of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representations from larger (teacher) models into smaller (student) models, enabling deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain mismatch. Across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings, distillation has expanded from logits matching to a diverse toolbox that includes feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, online and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and stabilizes student training, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability and selection of data, and defenses against transferred biases and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a configurable component within compression pipelines, pairing distilled signals with task- and deployment-aware engineering.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broad, practically driven family of methods that transfer predictive behavior, internal representations, or structured information from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, channel- and layer-wise objectives, self- and multi-teacher designs, data-free and few-shot protocols, and adversarial or generator-based data synthesis. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful data and training practices, distillation often preserves much of the teacher's performance and can add functional guarantees (robustness, low-precision accuracy, privacy-aware releases). Key limitations include dependence on teacher quality, student capacity and architectural alignment, distributional mismatch or limited data, and the risk of propagating teacher errors or biases, motivating continued work on principled objectives, data strategies, and deployment-aware pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Flexible, but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective and adaptable framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure) and training paradigms (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), enabling substantial reductions in inference cost when integrated with complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, available data (or the ability to synthesize it), and deliberate mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, distribution shift, and degraded performance on rare outputs. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful when designed and combined with other methods, but requiring task‑aware engineering and explicit safeguards to be reliable in practice.

papers_seen.author: Durham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically indispensable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count. Its effectiveness depends on deliberate choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student design and capacity alignment, data availability and selection, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe, KD delivers the most reliable and deployable gains.

papers_seen.author: Phelps
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When applied as a configurable component of an end-to-end compression pipeline—aligned with appropriate distillation targets, data strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search—KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of the teacher performance. However, its effectiveness is conditional on factors including teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and augmentation strategy, optimization practices, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and robustness failures. Careful, task-aware design and integrated pipelines are therefore required for reliable deployment and continued research into data-free distillation, bias mitigation, and teacher–student co‑design remains crucial.

papers_seen.author: Spence
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques that should be treated as an essential, task-aware component of model-compression pipelines rather than a one-size-fits-all solution. Properly designed KD—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, selecting or synthesizing suitable data, and integrating complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search—regularly yields compact models that preserve most teacher performance for deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. However, KD has predictable failure modes (teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare outputs) that require explicit mitigation and evaluation in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Configurable, but Insufficient — A Practical Position for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. As a practical tool it enables substantial efficiency gains across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks and supports privacy- and data-constrained settings. However, KD alone does not guarantee preservation of all important behaviors: success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student compatibility, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression methods. Therefore KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a one-size-fits-all solution.

papers_seen.author: Mcdaniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD is effective across modalities when treated as a configurable toolbox—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, curricula), and how to handle data constraints (augmentation, data-free synthesis, federated protocols). KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, but it is context-dependent: limitations include teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and difficulties with rare/long-tail phenomena. Best practice is to use KD as a principled component of an integrated compression pipeline, paired with task-aware design choices and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Grimes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad array of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps), protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, data-free and federated regimes), and integrations with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search) have been developed.
