papers_seen.author: Rosales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Component of Integrated Model Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Rather than a standalone cure, KD is most effective when treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that aligns distilled signals, teacher–student capacity, and data strategy, and that combines distillation with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Responsible deployment requires addressing known failure modes—data scarcity and distribution shift, capacity mismatch, degraded low-frequency behavior, and bias/privacy risks—through targeted remedies and evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD provides flexible transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals), supports data-limited and privacy-sensitive regimes via synthetic- or generator-based approaches, and interoperates with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet latency and memory constraints. Nevertheless, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student alignment, data and capacity matching, and explicit mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks, so it should be used as a configurable component within broader compression and deployment pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, flexible family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models. KD routinely delivers major efficiency gains (reduced FLOPs, latency, memory) while preserving much of teacher performance across vision and NLP tasks, and it integrates naturally with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distillation signals and data regime, and explicit handling of biases, robustness, and low‑frequency behaviors. Thus KD should be adopted as a core, configurable first‑line strategy within an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than as a one‑shot solution.

papers_seen.author: Shah
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically essential family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. KD supports multiple transfer targets and training protocols, is routinely combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and has been applied across modalities (language, vision, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks). Its empirical success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and careful design of what and how to transfer; persistent challenges include robustness, privacy, and reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to layer- and feature-level alignment, attention transfer, adversarial/contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free synthesis—regularly enable substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success requires matching distillation objectives to task and student capacity, choosing appropriate data strategies, and integrating KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Important open issues include optimization and capacity gaps, teacher-bias transfer, limited- or no-data scenarios, domain shift, privacy guarantees, and automated teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Oconnell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. When designed as part of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline — integrating pretraining, multi-signal transfer (logits, features, relational signals), data strategies, and compatible architecture choices — KD can preserve most teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its effectiveness is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the distilled signals and data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases or rare-case failures. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the practical core of modern model-compression toolkits, outlines concrete mechanisms by which it helps, surveys domain- and task-specific variants that address common failure modes, and summarizes actionable design principles for robust, responsible deployment.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft targets/logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, contrastive or adversarial objectives) and in varied protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co‑distillation, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free and federated regimes). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains shows KD frequently restores a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends critically on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as teacher-error propagation, bias transfer, and degraded low‑frequency behaviour. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and careful data/objective choices—to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Buchanan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Context‑Aware, and Insufficient Alone for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques that reliably improves the efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs of deep models across modalities. KD enables deployment by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, and it supports many training protocols and transfer targets. However, KD is not a standalone solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability or synthesis of suitable data, and careful mitigation of failure modes (distribution shift, low-frequency degradation, and bias propagation). Therefore, for robust real-world deployment KD should be treated as a configurable, task‑aware core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design), teacher–student co‑design, and data strategies tailored to the application.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical paradigm for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and workflows — including soft-logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-based training — has been developed and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, graphs) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, ranking, and more). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables deployment in resource- and latency-constrained settings while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher-student compatibility, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization mismatch, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible tool for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Empirical work across vision, language, and generative tasks shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing latency and resource use, but its effectiveness is sensitive to teacher–student design, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and complementary compression choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure: used well it unlocks substantial deployment gains; used alone or without task-aware design it can propagate teacher errors, struggle on rare phenomena, and fail under data or capacity mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for transferring functionality from large teacher models to smaller students so that compressed models retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and communication. KD covers a spectrum of techniques—from soft-target matching to internal representation transfer, multi-teacher/online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and architecture-aware solutions such as task-adaptive compression—and integrates naturally with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). When implemented with care about teacher selection, data selection or synthesis, and representation alignment, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing models across modalities; when misapplied it can propagate teacher errors, amplify biases, or fail due to optimization and data-mismatch issues. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-order engineering primitive for model compression in deep learning and NLP, and outlines recommended practices and known limitations to guide responsible adoption.

papers_seen.author: Lyons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD reliably reduces model size and latency while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and architecture-aware choices are selected for the deployment context. However, KD is not a universal solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis methods, and mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks. The most consistent practical outcomes come from treating KD as a configurable component within integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-aware distillation signals, augmentation or data-free techniques, and complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Class, Task-Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Frye
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (including ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods range from soft‑target (logit) matching to intermediate‑feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and include online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free/zero‑shot, and federated variants. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, generation, and specialized domains shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while greatly reducing inference cost and memory, but its effectiveness is highly context dependent and typically requires integration with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful teacher–student alignment, and data strategies to avoid failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, degraded long‑tail behavior, and transferred biases.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large, high‑capacity teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative and multimodal tasks, KD has been adapted into many targets and training regimes and is most effective when integrated with architecture‑aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the empirical strengths of KD, the principal methods and protocols, common limitations, and practical design patterns that guide successful compression and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational constraints), can be adapted to data‑limited and data‑free regimes, and combines productively with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). However, reliable deployment requires task‑aware design: selecting appropriate distillation objectives, aligning teacher and student capacities and architectures, addressing data regimes and privacy constraints, and mitigating failure modes such as bias transfer and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena. Treated as a configurable core of compression pipelines and paired with targeted algorithmic and engineering practices, KD enables practical, deployable model compression across modalities and settings.

papers_seen.author: Lester
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically important family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, multimodal, and constrained-deployment settings, KD uses diverse transfer targets and training protocols to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals, student capacity, and data strategies to task and deployment constraints and on integrating KD with complementary compression methods and privacy-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Fletcher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have evolved from a simple teacher-to-student logits-matching recipe into a broad toolbox for producing compact, efficient, and adaptable models in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Research has produced a range of practical methods—logit and feature matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware variants, and federated or online protocols—and has clarified connections to regularization, ensemble learning, and optimization. Empirical work shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of the teacher's performance, though gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and adaptation to deployment constraints. This synthesis summarizes core methods, theoretical insights, empirical findings, practical considerations, and open challenges that shape current best practice for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-faceted framework for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory use, and latency while retaining task performance. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and across multiple training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when paired with appropriate teacher–student design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives, but key limitations remain around data scarcity, teacher–student mismatch, transfer of undesirable behaviors, and insufficient theoretical understanding of what to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Gould
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence across vision, speech, and language shows KD routinely improves accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, but its success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data strategies. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Wyatt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a mature and practical set of techniques for converting large, high‑performing models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows that distillation—when applied with task awareness, appropriate choice of distilled signals, and complementary compression techniques—can recover much of teacher performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, and privacy. However, its success is conditional on teacher quality, data regimes, teacher–student alignment, and explicit mitigation of biases and low‑frequency failures; therefore, distillation should be integrated into end‑to‑end compression pipelines and not treated as a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. The literature develops multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline multi-stage, online, self-distillation, data-free/generative, adversarial), and application-specific adaptations (NLP transformer compression, vision, speech, graph models, federated and privacy-aware settings). Empirical work shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, data availability, and distributional or fairness concerns. Practical success generally requires matching the distillation objective to the task, handling data limitations with augmentation or synthetic generators, and integrating KD into a broader compression portfolio (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, efficient students by transferring information from teachers via outputs, internal representations, or relational signals. KD is broadly applicable across modalities and settings and is most effective when combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods. Despite strong empirical successes, important practical and theoretical challenges remain—teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity or scarcity, transferred biases, robustness under distribution shift, and privacy constraints—motivating targeted algorithmic and systems-level remedies and further study.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to satisfy deployment constraints such as latency, memory, compute, and privacy. KD includes a wide set of objectives and training protocols (logits/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, online/multi-teacher schemes, and data‑free or synthesized-data approaches). Empirical work shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance when it is matched to student capacity and data regimes and when it is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). At the same time, KD has clear limits—teacher–student mismatch, scarce or mismatched data, propagation of teacher errors and biases, and difficulty preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors—so best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline with explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Integrated Framework for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD works across modalities, supports deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and also acts as a regularizer; however, it has concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful teacher–student design. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely used family of methods for producing compact, deployable deep models by transferring behavior and internal information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft‑target matching into a diverse toolbox—logit/soft-label transfer, intermediate‑feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and self‑distillation, and data‑free or privacy‑aware protocols—and is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance but its success is context dependent: it requires attention to teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and selection or synthesis, and active mitigation of failure modes such as teacher error/bias propagation, distribution shift, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Shepherd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically supported toolkit for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (logit/soft-target matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-aware workflows) consistently enable favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and match of data, and distribution shift shape outcomes. For robust, production-ready compression, KD should be configured and combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design), data strategies, and task-aware safeguards against bias and low-frequency failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or differently structured models to smaller or more efficient ones, reducing computational cost and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings. Approaches vary in what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate representations, feature maps, attention or decision-boundary information), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, ensemble distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving setups), and how training data or augmentation is used. Empirical results across computer vision, speech/lipreading, retrieval, translation, reading comprehension, CTR prediction, federated learning, GANs, NAS, and Transformer compression show that appropriate combination of distillation objective, data strategy, and model design can yield large gains in efficiency with modest or no loss in accuracy. Practical factors that shape success include teacher strength and mismatch to the student, the complexity of distilled data, the role of pre-training for compact models, targeted selection or augmentation of distillation samples, and orthogonal compression techniques such as structured pruning.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student logits-matching recipe into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing models and enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware. Modern KD variants transfer not only soft labels but also internal and feature representations, employ multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, and integrate with federated and data-constrained workflows. When matched to the task (e.g., feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP, projector adapters for mismatched architectures, or privacy-aware ensembles for federated settings), KD enables small models to approximate or sometimes match larger teachers while offering routes to improved robustness and inclusivity. However, realizing these gains requires attention to teacher quality, capacity gaps, the form of distilled information, and sample-wise effects of soft targets. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable component of model-compression pipelines and present evidence-based practical recommendations for when and how to apply its variants.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for converting high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to feature-, attention-, and relation-level alignment, as well as online, ensemble, and data-free variants—have enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Practical application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to generate or select data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

However, KD is context dependent: its success hinges on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and mitigation of failure modes. papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Necessary but Insufficient Core for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework that transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving much of the teacher's performance. KD methods include logit/soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or adversarial example synthesis. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment on resource-constrained platforms; however, KD alone does not resolve challenges such as teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity and scarcity, preservation of rare-token or long-tail behavior, and the transfer of teacher biases. Effective compression pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable core component that must be combined with task-aware engineering, complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, hardware-aware design), and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable mechanism for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its objectives, data, and mappings are chosen with the target task and student capacity in mind; but KD alone does not guarantee production-ready compression. Reliable deployment requires integrating distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design), careful data and teacher selection, layer and projector design, and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and rare-behavior transfer.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.
