papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized student models. A rich set of transfer targets and protocols—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to feature- and attention-level alignment, relational/contrastive objectives, and data- or generator-based synthesis—has been developed and successfully applied across vision, language, speech, recommender systems, and multimodal domains. Practical KD pipelines typically combine distillation with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and projector layers), and their success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and explicit mitigations for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Remaining challenges include principled theory linking teacher signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, privacy-aware protocols, and preserving rare or structured behaviors under compression.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. Across vision, language, and generative settings, KD offers multiple transfer targets and protocols that enable meaningful reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a turnkey cure: its practical success requires careful, task‑aware choices about which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity and architecture, how to handle limited or private data, and how to pair distillation with complementary compression primitives and safeguards for rare-case behavior and bias. Treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline, KD delivers robust, deployable gains; remaining challenges motivate continued work on principled objectives, data‑efficient and privacy‑aware protocols, and reliable long‑tail preservation.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

Reliable deployment requires integrating distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design), careful data and teacher selection, layer and projector design, and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and rare-behavior transfer.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied, practical framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. KD encompasses diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data‑free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and distributional failures.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal settings. Responsible deployment requires attention to robustness, fairness, privacy, and teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. The practical effectiveness of KD depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability, and mitigation of bias or robustness issues.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Evidence and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. Across vision, language, graph, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD methods vary in what they transfer (soft targets, intermediate features, attention or relational structure, contrastive signals) and how they are applied (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance and can enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware; however, practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data and augmentation strategies, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning and quantization. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels — soft targets (logits), intermediate representations, attention and relational structure, and contrastive objectives — and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, pretraining, and architecture adaptation. Practical success is conditional on teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful optimization and evaluation to avoid propagating teacher artifacts, degrading rare-case behavior, or failing under distribution shift. The field shows strong empirical gains across vision, language, speech, recommendation, generative, and multimodal tasks, while open problems remain in theory, heterogeneous architectures, privacy-aware protocols, and robust transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities when combined with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch create failure modes that require deliberate mitigation and integrated design.

papers_seen.author: Gordon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of methods for producing compact models from larger teachers. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows KD can deliver large efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity, data and objective design, and complementary compression choices.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their capabilities. KD enables deployment across modalities and constrained environments, and empirical work shows it can approach teacher performance when combined with complementary techniques. However, KD is not a universal solution: it can propagate teacher errors and biases, struggle under data scarcity or mismatch, and require careful choices of distilled targets, architectures, and training schedules. To realize KD's benefits in production and research settings, practitioners should pair distillation with targeted remedies—representation-aware objectives, data-and-curriculum strategies, ensemble or adversarial schemes, and fairness or privacy interventions—tailored to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lyons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD reliably reduces model size and latency while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and architecture-aware choices are selected for the deployment context. However, KD is not a universal solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis methods, and mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks. The most consistent practical outcomes come from treating KD as a configurable component within integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-aware distillation signals, augmentation or data-free techniques, and complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable component of a compression pipeline and adapted to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints, KD reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on signal selection, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and integration with complementary compression methods; responsible use requires mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, low‑frequency degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures, and they operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align layers, and how to handle limited or private data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, robustness and fairness transfer, data-free/privacy-preserving distillation, and principled selection of distilled signals.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD operates at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structures—and is effective across modalities (vision, language, speech, and translation) when adapted to task constraints. KD achieves substantial reductions in latency and model size while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate transferred biases and low-frequency or out-of-distribution failures. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, central component of an integrated compression and deployment pipeline rather than as a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Potency, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing and adapting large neural models for deployment, cross-task transfer, federated settings, and multi-modal scenarios. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or module replacement), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and compute with modest accuracy loss. However, gains are not automatic: careful choice of what to distill (outputs, intermediate representations, or selected samples), how to mix hard/soft signals, and how to adapt KD to distributed or data-free regimes strongly affects outcomes. I argue that KD is most effective when it is task-aware, representation-aware, and integrated with other compression methods, and that future work should prioritize principled selection of distilled knowledge, robustness to teacher imperfections, and practical protocols for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Bishop
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for producing compact, faster models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, retrieval, and generative tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher schemes—have been developed and combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of transferred errors and rare-output degradation. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, practical guidance, and open challenges for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Harper
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Across vision, language, speech, retrieval, graph, and generative tasks, KD variants transfer information at output and internal levels and are commonly integrated with complementary compression primitives. Empirical evidence shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable deployment on resource-constrained hardware, but success is context-dependent and requires careful design around what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and mitigation of bias, privacy, and rare‑phenomena degradation.

papers_seen.author: Schmidt
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. A large and consistent body of work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities when the distilled signals, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen carefully. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness is context-dependent: it is bounded by data availability, teacher quality, capacity mismatch, and risks of transferring undesirable behaviors, so it is best applied as part of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Richardson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD methods vary in what they transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational/contrastive signals) and how they train (offline teacher–student, online/self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free). Empirical studies show KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data strategy, and careful integration with other compression primitives. Treating KD as a configurable core within an integrated, deployment‑aware compression pipeline yields the most reliable practical outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Blankenship
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable, task‑aware component of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with complementary methods and data strategies, KD enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while preserving much of teacher performance; however, realizing these benefits requires careful design to mitigate limitations such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and transferred biases.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: A Central but Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practically effective set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, distillation yields substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often recovering much of teacher performance. However, its success is highly context dependent: outcomes hinge on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and training protocol, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. For robust, fair, and production-ready compression, distillation should be deployed as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that combine architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, privacy, and long‑tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Serrano
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal settings, KD methods — from soft‑target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi‑teacher and online schemes, and data‑free or privacy‑aware protocols — consistently improve accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when combined with task‑aware design and complementary compression techniques. Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful attention to teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, what signals are transferred and how layers are mapped, data availability or synthesis strategies, and interventions to mitigate bias, rare‑token degradation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best Used within Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applicable and practically effective toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD can recover much of teacher performance, enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, and be extended across logits, feature, attention, and data‑free paradigms. Its effectiveness, however, is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and selection of distillation data, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable, task‑aware component that must be combined with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies, and robustness/fairness safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Clayton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–performance tradeoffs, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate data. For robust production use, KD should be treated as a configurable, task‑aware core element embedded in integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-level objectives, projector or layer‑mapping modules, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning and quantization. Careful engineering is required to avoid propagating teacher errors or biases and to preserve rare or low‑frequency behaviors under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—from logits (soft-target) transfer to intermediate-feature, attention/relational, contrastive, adversarial, multi-teacher, and data-free protocols—enable reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. Successful distillation depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data availability; practitioners generally combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training protocols. Persistent challenges include capacity and optimization mismatch, data- or privacy-constrained regimes, reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Promising directions emphasize task-aware signal selection, flexible layer mappings, multi-teacher or ensemble designs, adversarial/data-free sample synthesis, and integrated pipelines that co-design KD with other compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, widely used toolbox to transfer behavior and representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, resource-efficient students. The approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or generated samples), whether original training data are available, and whether the objective emphasizes efficiency, privacy, robustness, or interpretability. Across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks, carefully designed distillation objectives and training pipelines—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search—produce compact models that approach teacher performance under deployment constraints. Key practical challenges are capacity and optimization mismatch between teacher and student, data- and privacy-limited settings, distribution shift and low-frequency phenomena, and the risk of transferring undesirable teacher traits; promising responses include task-aware filtering of teacher signals, multi-layer mapping strategies, data-free sample synthesis, and privacy-preserving noise mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Insufficient — A Practical Position for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practically proven strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployable students across vision and language tasks. While distilled students often recover much of teacher performance, distillation alone is not a complete solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and careful selection of what to transfer. In practice, distillation should be treated as a configurable core of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that integrates complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), explicit fairness and robustness interventions, and data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Crawford
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods that transfer knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses diverse transfer targets and training protocols and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design. Empirical evidence across modalities shows substantial efficiency gains, but persistent challenges—data limitations, capacity mismatch, transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors, and degradation on long-tail phenomena—motivate careful pipeline design and continued research on robust, privacy-aware, and hardware-aware distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Burns
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD produces large practical gains when it is treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—and when practitioners attend to teacher–student capacity, data regime, and optimization design. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with low-frequency phenomena, and fail under data scarcity or severe teacher–student mismatch. Therefore the recommended position is to adopt KD as the default first-line compression strategy, but to explicitly pair it with complementary methods and safeguards tailored to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hayden
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded framework for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary teacher models into compact students. KD methods include soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, data-free or zero-shot schemes, and self-distillation. Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance when combined with suitable data strategies, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and safeguards against transferred artifacts, distributional mismatch, and social harms. The practical consensus treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a plug-and-play solution.

papers_seen.author: Tyler
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical toolbox for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. The literature provides a diverse set of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive signals), training protocols (offline multi-stage, online and self-distillation, multi-teacher and teacher-annealed schedules), and data strategies (augmentation, data-free synthesis, adversarial generation), often combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search). Empirical results show KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints, but outcomes are highly context-dependent: they hinge on teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and distribution of data, task-specific objectives, and mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases or long-tail degradation. Outstanding challenges include principled theory linking teacher signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under data or device heterogeneity and privacy constraints, and automated, hardware-aware co-design of teacher–student pairs and compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Campbell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Flexible, but Not Panacea Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students and for transferring task- or modality-specific capabilities. KD supports many transfer targets and training protocols and can be combined with pruning, quantization, pretraining, and data synthesis to meet deployment constraints. However, reliable outcomes require careful teacher–student design, attention to data and privacy constraints, and targeted solutions for failure modes such as distribution shift, optimization mismatch, and preserved low-frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Ewing
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically validated approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs, but its effectiveness is highly context dependent: it requires careful choices about what signals to transfer, alignment between teacher and student, and data strategies, and it is most reliable when integrated with complementary compression techniques and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: Compressing Deep Graph Neural Networks via Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have been shown to be expressive for modeling graph-structured data. Nevertheless, the over-stacked architecture of deep graph models makes it difficult to deploy and rapidly test on mobile or embedded systems. To compress over-stacked GNNs, knowledge distillation via a teacher-student architecture turns out to be an effective technique, where the key step is to measure the discrepancy between teacher and student networks with predefined distance functions. However, using the same distance for graphs of various structures may be unfit, and the optimal distance formulation is hard to determine. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel Adversarial Knowledge Distillation framework for graph models named GraphAKD, which adversarially trains a discriminator and a generator to adaptively detect and decrease the discrepancy. Specifically, noticing that the well-captured inter-node and inter-class correlations favor the success of deep GNNs, we propose to criticize the inherited knowledge from node-level and class-level views with a trainable discriminator. The discriminator distinguishes between teacher knowledge and what the student inherits, while the student GNN works as a generator and aims to fool the discriminator. To our best knowledge, GraphAKD is the first to introduce adversarial training to knowledge distillation in graph domains. Experiments on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks demonstrate that GraphAKD improves the student performance by a large margin. The results imply that GraphAKD can precisely transfer knowledge from a complicated teacher GNN to a compact student GNN.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default First‑Line Tool within Integrated Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated method for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when configured to transfer appropriate signals (logits, features, attention, relations) and combined with complementary compression primitives. However, KD is context dependent: teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of bias and rare‑case degradation matter. I argue KD should serve as the default first‑line compression mechanism, but always as a configurable component of an integrated pipeline that explicitly addresses data regimes, architecture co‑design, and fairness/robustness safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Duran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. When applied as a configurable element within integrated compression pipelines and matched to task, data, and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields favorable trade‑offs between accuracy, latency, and resource use. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and fidelity, and careful handling of robustness, fairness, and privacy concerns. Responsible application therefore treats KD as a core tool combined with complementary methods and targeted safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical toolkit for converting large teacher models or ensembles into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, privacy, and deployment constraints. A rich family of distillation targets and training protocols has emerged—soft logits, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, data‑free and adversarial synthesis, and federated or online variants. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with task‑aware choices about signals to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, and appropriate data strategies, but it has well-documented limits (capacity mismatch, teacher error/bias propagation, degraded long‑tail/rare-token behavior, distribution shift, and data- or privacy-limited regimes). Robust, deployable compression therefore treats KD as a configurable core component embedded in an integrated pipeline with complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and explicit safeguards and evaluation for fairness, robustness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Tyler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster, or deployment‑specialized student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and federated settings, KD methods—including soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or data‑free generation, and self- or online‑distillation—enable substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on aligning distillation signals to student capacity and task requirements, selecting or synthesizing suitable data, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Important limitations remain (teacher–student capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, failures on low‑frequency phenomena, and distribution shift), so KD is best used as a configurable component within an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline with explicit evaluation of robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a diverse set of methods for transferring behavior and representations from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques range from matching soft output distributions to aligning intermediate features, transferring relational structure, adversarial or data‑free supervision, and teacher/student co‑design; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search, KD forms a central part of modern compression pipelines. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently retain much of teacher performance and can improve generalization, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware engineering to address teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Key
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger, often ensemble, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at the logit level, at intermediate representation and attention levels, and via relational or contrastive objectives; they are routinely combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis. Empirically, well-designed distillation pipelines can produce compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance, enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy and device constraints. Success depends on choices about what and how to transfer, the quality and alignment of teacher and student, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data; important open problems remain around distribution shift, bias/fairness transfer, low-frequency behavior, and principled theoretical understanding.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed as part of a task-aware compression pipeline that includes appropriate distillation targets, data strategies, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), KD can preserve most of a teacher’s performance while meeting real-world constraints on latency, memory, and privacy. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the signals and data used for transfer, and careful mitigation of transferred biases and robustness failures. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable, evidence-driven toolkit that must be tailored to specific tasks and constraints.

papers_seen.author: Browning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated technique for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, recommender, and multimodal tasks. KD routinely delivers substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss when applied with task- and capacity-aware design, but it is not a universal remedy: its success depends on choices of transfer signal, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and loss of rare behaviors. For reliable production use, KD should be treated as a configurable core element within hybrid compression pipelines that include pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, a diverse toolbox of distillation targets, training protocols, and data strategies has been developed. Practical deployment typically treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) while attending to data regimes, teacher–student alignment, and risks such as transferred bias and degraded behavior on rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD provides flexible transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals), supports data-limited and privacy-sensitive regimes via synthetic- or generator-based approaches, and interoperates with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet latency and memory constraints. Nevertheless, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student alignment, data and capacity matching, and explicit mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks, so it should be used as a configurable component within broader compression and deployment pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster ones while transferring performance and often additional properties such as robustness or cross-domain adaptability. Evidence across vision, language, graph, and sequential domains shows KD enables deployable models for latency- and resource-constrained settings, supports continual and federated learning, and can be combined with pruning, architecture search, and adversarial strategies. However, distillation is not a universal panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, interact nontrivially with regularization strategies, and requires careful alignment of inputs, representations, and objectives. Best practice is to treat KD as a family of tools (logit, intermediate-layer, feature, adversarial, data-driven, self-distillation) and to adapt the distillation design to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Kerr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When designed with task-aware objectives, appropriate teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression primitives, KD routinely yields large efficiency gains while preserving predictive quality. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on choices of what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability, and it requires explicit strategies to avoid propagating teacher errors or losing rare/low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Configurable First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile, and empirically supported family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. It reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, the data regime, and deployment constraints. Therefore KD should be adopted as a first‑line, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines, combined with complementary methods and targeted safeguards to address known failure modes and domain-specific challenges.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and versatile toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A broad family of distillation objectives and protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, contrastive, adversarial, and data‑free approaches—and KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design. Success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and explicit handling of distribution shift, low-frequency behaviors, privacy, and architecture heterogeneity.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, or specialized models. When designed around task constraints, student capacity, and available data, KD preserves much of a teacher's capabilities while enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy limits. Its greatest value comes from treating distillation as a configurable toolkit—combining soft-targets, representation matching, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and multi-teacher or self-distillation—with complementary compression techniques to meet real-world constraints. Success requires careful handling of teacher–student alignment, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias transfer, but a task-aware, hybrid pipeline makes KD one of the most practical routes to effective model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Campbell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger, more accurate, or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Over the past decade KD has broadened from matching teacher output probabilities to a diverse set of objectives that include internal representation matching, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and online or self-distillation schedules. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training pipelines, distillation enables deployment of high-performing models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on careful design choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transferred errors, biases, and distributional brittleness.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Necessary but Insufficient Core for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework that transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving much of the teacher's performance. KD methods include logit/soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or adversarial example synthesis. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment on resource-constrained platforms; however, KD alone does not resolve challenges such as teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity and scarcity, preservation of rare-token or long-tail behavior, and the transfer of teacher biases. Effective compression pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable core component that must be combined with task-aware engineering, complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, hardware-aware design), and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling deployable systems under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD methods span soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. Empirical evidence shows KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs, but reliable deployment requires task- and data-aware design, attention to teacher–student compatibility, and combination with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.
