papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. It operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals, contrastive and adversarial objectives) and is most effective when tailored to the task, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit protocols to mitigate failure modes such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and the transfer of biases or private information. Responsible application requires task-aware teacher–student design, data strategies (including data-free or few-shot methods when necessary), and monitoring for degraded behavior on low-frequency or structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Vaughan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Conditional, and Best Used as Part of an Integrated Compression Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely used set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD can transfer final outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure and can be run in offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free regimes. Empirically, when teacher quality, student capacity, distillation signals, and data strategies are well matched to the task and deployment constraints, distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while achieving substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on careful teacher–student co‑design, judicious selection of transfer signals, appropriate data or synthetic-data strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as capacity mismatch, transferred biases, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models by transferring information from larger or specialized models. It supports a broad range of objectives beyond raw compression—improving robustness, enabling domain adaptation, supporting privacy-aware or federated workflows, and permitting deployment on constrained hardware. KD methods range from simple soft-label matching to richer transfers of intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational or contrastive structure. While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, alignment between teacher and student, data availability and distribution, and the choice of signals and losses. When applied with attention to these constraints and combined sensibly with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), KD is a practical foundational technique for real-world model compression in vision, language, and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD operates via many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, adversarial or data‑free generation, and online or multi‑teacher training—and is typically combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet practical latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware design, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful engineering to avoid failure modes such as teacher error transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, Practical Guidance, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for producing compact models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD spans outputs-only approaches and a wide range of internal-signal targets, supports offline and online protocols, and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and task-aware data strategies. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but success is context dependent: it requires careful teacher–student alignment, appropriate distillation signals and data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagated teacher errors and biases, degraded long-tail/rare-token behavior, distribution shift, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hughes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and deployment-ready models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. Across soft-target matching, internal-representation alignment, attention and relational signals, and data-synthesis strategies, KD is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, pretraining, and architecture-aware design to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical studies show KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance, but its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and selection, and task-aware objective design; persistent challenges include preserving low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, handling heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, and building principled theory that predicts when specific distillation signals will help.

papers_seen.author: Blevins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides a practical, flexible pathway to produce compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. Its empirical success across modalities and tasks is clear, but reliable deployment requires co‑design of teacher and student, careful choice of transfer signals, attention to data regimes, and integration with complementary compression and safeguarding techniques. Treating distillation as a configurable core—not a turnkey solution—yields the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or differently structured models to smaller or more efficient ones, reducing computational cost and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings. Approaches vary in what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate representations, feature maps, attention or decision-boundary information), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, ensemble distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving setups), and how training data or augmentation is used. Empirical results across computer vision, speech/lipreading, retrieval, translation, reading comprehension, CTR prediction, federated learning, GANs, NAS, and Transformer compression show that appropriate combination of distillation objective, data strategy, and model design can yield large gains in efficiency with modest or no loss in accuracy. Practical factors that shape success include teacher strength and mismatch to the student, the complexity of distilled data, the role of pre-training for compact models, targeted selection or augmentation of distillation samples, and orthogonal compression techniques such as structured pruning.

papers_seen.author: Pitts

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. KD techniques span soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level objectives, relational/contrastive signals, and protocols such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free variants. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks KD routinely reduces latency, memory, and compute while recovering much of teacher performance, but its success is context-dependent: outcomes hinge on signal choice, teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression primitives. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of broader compression pipelines, guided by task-aware design, teacher–student co‑engineering, and targeted mitigations for bias, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Pennington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used and flexible approach for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models in deep learning and NLP. Over the past decade a wide family of KD variants has been developed — logits/soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble and multi-teacher schemes, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and layer-mapping strategies — and KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture or neural architecture search). Empirical evidence shows that KD often recovers a large share of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, which data to use or synthesize, and how to mitigate failure modes such as transferred bias, teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, and degraded modeling of low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and federative settings, distillation can preserve much of a teacher's predictive quality while reducing inference latency, memory footprint, and communication costs. Different distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, contrastive signals) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot) make KD adaptable to diverse deployment constraints. At the same time, distillation has well-documented failure modes—transfer of teacher biases, degradation on rare or low-frequency phenomena, sensitivity to data heterogeneity and teacher–student capacity mismatch—and practical success depends on task-aware design choices and often combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. The field thus treats KD as a multifaceted, application-driven set of methods whose best practice is to match signals, data, and student capacity to deployment needs while applying targeted mitigations for privacy, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for transferring behaviors and representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while preserving much of task performance. KD variants operate on soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure, and can run in offline, online, data‑free, or federated regimes. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often recovers most of a teacher’s accuracy and can improve student generalization or robustness when combined with complementary compression methods (quantization, pruning, architecture adaptation) and careful data and training strategies. However, KD is context sensitive: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, selection of distilled signals and layer mappings, availability and curation of data (or synthetic alternatives), and mitigation of failure modes like teacher bias, capacity mismatch, and degraded long‑tail behavior. Treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and applying targeted remedies (selective sample choices, projectors, teacher annealing, multi‑signal objectives) produces the most reliable practical results.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. The methods span output-level soft-targets, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and application-specific protocols such as online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data-free approaches. KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, memory, and deployment barriers, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit protections against transferred biases and degraded rare-output behavior. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and task-aware training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Bartlett
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, broadly applicable family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models from larger teacher models. KD operates over multiple signals (output logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure) and protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free or privacy‑aware schemes). Empirical evidence across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains shows that KD—particularly when combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and when guided by task‑aware objectives and data strategies—regularly yields favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs. However, KD is context dependent: its effectiveness hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and nature of distillation data, and explicit mitigations for bias, robustness, and domain shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a stand‑alone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate across multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure) and training paradigms (offline, online/multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free/adversarial synthesis). Empirical work shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and compute constraints, but its success is context‑dependent and typically benefits from integration with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic data, data‑free approaches), and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Burgess
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods include output-level supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, online and multi-teacher protocols, and progressive or task-aware procedures. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative and multimodal tasks shows that when KD is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task- and data-aware engineering, it often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing resource cost. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Important open challenges remain in principled selection of distillation targets, reliable transfer under data scarcity and distribution shift, avoiding propagation of teacher biases and rare-token degradation, and automated, hardware-aware co-design.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Wolf
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact models from larger teachers and ensembles. It frequently yields strong efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance, but its reliability depends on task‑aware design, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods. Responsible deployment of KD requires explicit safeguards for bias, distributional shift, and rare behaviours.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers information at multiple levels—soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational structure, or synthesized examples—and can be organized in diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free regimes). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design, KD routinely produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. However, KD’s success is strongly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and calibration, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and match of distillation data (or quality of synthetic surrogates), and careful objective and pipeline design to avoid propagating teacher errors or degrading long‑tail behaviour. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline, not a universal panacea.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models. KD variants — from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate‑feature and relational objectives, multi‑teacher and online regimes, and data‑free or privacy-aware methods — routinely yield strong accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs when combined with task‑aware design and complementary compression primitives. However, KD’s practical success is conditional on careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the signals to transfer, and data strategies; thus KD should be used as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines rather than as a plug‑and‑play cure.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Oconnell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. When designed as part of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline — integrating pretraining, multi-signal transfer (logits, features, relational signals), data strategies, and compatible architecture choices — KD can preserve most teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its effectiveness is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the distilled signals and data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases or rare-case failures. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the practical core of modern model-compression toolkits, outlines concrete mechanisms by which it helps, surveys domain- and task-specific variants that address common failure modes, and summarizes actionable design principles for robust, responsible deployment.

papers_seen.author: Curry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from large teacher models into smaller student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Research and practice have developed a diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, using contrastive/relational objectives, generating or selecting distillation data, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combining KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, speech, and multimodal tasks shows distilled students frequently recover much of teacher performance, though effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and alignment of objectives and representations. Key open problems include reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors, robust distillation under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, principled teacher selection and co-design, and automated, task-aware distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a diverse set of practical techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce memory, latency, and computational cost while retaining much of teacher performance. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-teaching, and data-aware or data-free variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines that also include pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation; its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability (or synthesis), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred errors, bias, and degradation on rare outputs. Important open directions include principled selection of distilled signals, privacy-preserving and data-free distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation workflows.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Fields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool — Argument for Integrated, Context‑Aware Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD’s effectiveness is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability or synthesis of suitable training data. For robust, real‑world compression, KD should be treated as a configurable component within an integrated pipeline that combines representation-level transfer, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture‑aware compression (pruning, quantization, or search), together with explicit safeguards for bias, robustness, and low‑frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Conditional Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD succeeds by transferring rich forms of information — soft logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive structure, and even synthesized data — and by being combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not an automatic remedy: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and privacy constraints, and defenses against transferring teacher errors or low-frequency phenomena. Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component within a broader compression pipeline, and adopting practices such as layer- and task-aware objectives, multi-teacher confidence weighting, adversarial or decision-boundary sample generation, and data-aware synthesis or augmentation, yields the most reliable trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity. Remaining research directions include principled guidance for selecting which signals to transfer, robust privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Kline
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into compact student models. The literature provides a rich toolbox—output-level (soft targets), intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and variants such as multi-teacher, online/self-distillation, data‑free and meta‑learning approaches. Empirical and conceptual work agrees that KD is most effective when adapted to task constraints, student capacity, and data availability and when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design).

papers_seen.author: Hodge
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework that compresses large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal signals. A rich toolkit of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), training protocols (offline, online/mutual, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data approaches) and engineering practices (layer mapping, curriculum/weighting, and integration with pruning, quantization, or architecture search) has emerged. Empirically, KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains, but outcomes are context dependent: success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and careful choices about what and how to transfer. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable, task‑aware component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a single off‑the‑shelf recipe.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, distillation is used to transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from larger, more accurate teachers to smaller, faster students; it also appears within automated model search, pruning and distributed training workflows. Work in this area spans logit matching, representation-level objectives, data-free and few-shot regimes, multi-/online-teacher schemes, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy while enabling large reductions in memory and compute, but limitations remain around optimization, data availability, and the preservation or mitigation of undesirable biases.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often retaining much of teacher performance, but its success is context dependent: it requires task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data strategies (including synthetic or privacy‑aware data), and complementary compression primitives. The most reliable deployments treat KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a stand‑alone cure, and continuing research should prioritize robustness, fairness, privacy, and principled methods for heterogeneous and low‑data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a broadly applicable paradigm that enables deployment of large models across modalities, supports privacy- and resource-constrained federated scenarios, and improves generalization when combined with task- and architecture-specific techniques. Empirical evidence shows that KD alone yields large gains for small students, while hybrid approaches that distill internal representations, use curriculum or meta-learning, augment data, or jointly optimize architecture and distillation produce state-of-the-art trade-offs between size, speed, and task performance. KD is therefore a foundational tool for modern model compression strategies and should be used in concert with complementary methods (e.g., pretraining, low-precision numerics, structural compression, and privacy-aware distillation) to meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Roach
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods span output-level supervision (soft logits), intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive losses, adversarial and data-free generation, online and multi-teacher protocols, and self-distillation. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks shows KD frequently yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are carefully matched. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline alongside pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and calls for explicit strategies to mitigate teacher bias, handle data scarcity or privacy constraints, and maintain rare-token or long-tail behaviors. Remaining challenges include principled signal selection for heterogeneous architectures, robust and private distillation under non‑i.i.d. data, and automated, deployment‑aware teacher–student co‑design.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Galvan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Necessity, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are essential engineering primitives for making large deep models practical in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings. Empirical results across vision, language, and multimodal tasks show that carefully chosen distillation targets, training schedules, and data strategies enable small students to recover much of teacher performance. At the same time, important challenges remain—data heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency behavior preservation, and principled teacher selection—motivating focused research and deployment practices.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Across vision, language, graph, and generative modeling, KD methods vary by what is transferred (teacher logits, internal representations, attention, relational structure), how layers are aligned or projected, and how data constraints (limited access, privacy, or distribution shift) are handled. Empirical work demonstrates that combining output-level and representation-level objectives, using layer-mapping or projector modules, and adapting training data or curricula yields the best trade-offs between compactness and accuracy. Despite wide success, effective distillation requires careful choices about teacher quality, distilled signals, sample selection, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Order, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: I argue that knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first-order technique for compressing and adapting deep models for practical deployment in vision and language systems. KD's flexibility—supporting logits, intermediate features, relational signals, online/multi-teacher regimes, and data-free variants—lets practitioners address latency, memory, on-device inference, privacy, and domain adaptation constraints. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: its success depends on teacher quality, the choice of transfer signals, data availability (or synthetic data methods), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, low-frequency degradation, and distribution shift. Accordingly, KD should be used as a configurable toolkit combined with task-aware design, auxiliary compression methods, and deployment-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Configurable, but Insufficient — A Practical Position for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used approach for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. As a practical tool it enables substantial efficiency gains across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks and supports privacy- and data-constrained settings. However, KD alone does not guarantee preservation of all important behaviors: success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student compatibility, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression methods. Therefore KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a one-size-fits-all solution.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information beyond hard labels. Across logits-based soft-targets, intermediate-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free schemes, and architecture-aware strategies, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs in vision, language, retrieval, graphs, and generative tasks. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data and privacy constraints, and combination with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining gaps include robustness under distribution shift, preserving low-frequency/long-tail behavior, mitigating teacher artifacts and bias, and devising reliable procedures when original data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, latency, memory, and communication while often preserving much of task performance. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple logits/soft-target matching to include feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware data strategies. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, the choice and availability of distillation data (or synthesis strategies), and explicit mitigations for failure modes such as transferred bias, degraded rare-output behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Rose
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. KD encompasses many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free and privacy-aware variants). Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines appropriate distillation objectives with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies) and careful evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated set of techniques for producing smaller, deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains, KD methods and protocols—when combined with careful data, architecture, and deployment-aware decisions—regularly yield substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. Success is context dependent, and practical deployments pair KD with complementary compression primitives and targeted safeguards for robustness, privacy, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible approach for producing compact models from larger teachers that preserves much of their performance across tasks and modalities. Its strengths arise from multiple transfer mechanisms (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals) and from compatibility with complementary compression tools. However, KD is not automatic: success requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and integration with other compression methods. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component of modern model-deployment toolkits, with explicit practices to mitigate its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Gilbert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, versatile framework that reliably reduces inference cost and memory while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities. KD operates at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals), and is most effective when treated as a configurable, task-aware core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines pre‑training and architecture design with pruning, quantization, and data strategies. KD has clear strengths (efficiency gains, regularization-like benefits, applicability to privacy- and domain-constrained settings) but also concrete failure modes (capacity and optimization mismatch, teacher error propagation, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, distribution shift, and privacy/bias concerns). Practical deployment therefore requires explicit design choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to obtain or synthesize data, and how to combine KD with complementary compression and robustness measures.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD methods—ranging from soft‑logit matching to intermediate‑feature and attention transfers, adversarial or contrastive objectives, and multi‑teacher schemes—regularly enable large reductions in inference cost and parameter footprint while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD’s effectiveness is strongly dependent on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and optimization dynamics; therefore, reliable compression in practice requires combining KD with task‑aware design choices and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis) and explicit mitigation strategies for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, task‑aware toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners match soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data to train compact students. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and data strategies, and explicit teacher–student alignment; however, important limitations remain in distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, heterogeneous architectures, privacy and federated settings, and principled teacher selection. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open challenges distilled from the supplied literature.
