papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and recommender systems, KD methods have been developed to match outputs (soft targets), internal representations (features and attention), relational or contrastive signals, and task-specific rank or ordering information. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability (including data-free strategies), and integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Trade-offs include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and optimization challenges; many works propose curricula, student-friendly teacher training, or multi-teacher and online protocols to mitigate these issues. The field has matured into a central engineering primitive for deployment, while continuing to pursue principled transfer objectives, privacy-aware distillation, and robust domain- and architecture-aware pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Necessity, Limits, and a Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling reduced memory, lower-latency inference, and new capabilities such as task-adaptive compression, multi-task transfer, and interpretable surrogates. At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, dataset and distribution mismatches, teacher bias transfer, and design choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relational structure) strongly affect outcomes. The most reliable results come from combining KD with complementary techniques (teacher adaptation, selective or curriculum-driven sample selection, representation matching, low-precision numerics, and scaled training procedures) and from tailoring the procedure to task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of approaches for transferring information from large, expensive teacher models into smaller, efficient student models to reduce computation, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. Over the past decade these techniques have expanded from simple soft-target (logit) supervision to a broad, configurable toolkit that includes intermediate representation matching, attention and relational objectives, online and self-distillation, data‑free and adversarial synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment on constrained hardware, but outcomes depend critically on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and design of data for distillation, and mitigation strategies for transferred errors, distribution shift, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Synthesis of the Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller students. Across modalities and training protocols, distillation operates at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware design. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful objective and optimization design; important limitations include teacher error propagation, impaired modeling of low-frequency phenomena, and distribution-shift vulnerabilities.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive signals) and across diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data-free/privacy-aware schemes). When combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables large reductions in latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Its empirical success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Ford
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Conditional, and Best Integrated into Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile set of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models so that compact models can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD routinely improves efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across modalities, but its practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of appropriate data, and careful mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degraded low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Therefore KD should be treated as a configurable core component of integrated compression workflows—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—rather than a turnkey, standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Whitaker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. KD reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves much of teacher performance when engineered carefully. However, KD is not a universal cure: success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, available or synthetic data, and complementary compression choices (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Responsible, production-ready compression treats KD as the default core of an integrated pipeline, tuned to task constraints and guarded against failure modes such as transferred bias, degraded rare‑token behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models so the students meet latency, memory, compute, or privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. KD variants operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals) and across diverse data regimes (full-data, limited-data, and data-free). Empirical evidence shows KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when integrated into end-to-end compression pipelines that also use pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies. Practical deployment requires task- and capacity-aware design, careful teacher–student co‑design, and explicit safeguards for failure modes such as propagated bias, degraded low‑frequency behavior, and distribution shift; these remain active areas for research.

papers_seen.author: Durham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically indispensable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count. Its effectiveness depends on deliberate choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student design and capacity alignment, data availability and selection, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe, KD delivers the most reliable and deployable gains.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD techniques extend beyond matching logits: they include internal-representation distillation, adversarial and relational approaches, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware methods, and architecture-aware replacements. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve or even improve generalization, enable domain adaptation, and permit deployment under resource, privacy, or latency constraints—provided practitioners attend to known failure modes such as teacher bias, low-frequency lexical errors, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Romero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Conditional — The Case for an Integrated Compression Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. KD routinely delivers favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis strategies, and integration with complementary compression primitives. I argue KD should be treated as the central element of a task‑aware, validated compression pipeline rather than as a stand‑alone cure.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core with Clear Limits — Guidance for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely useful set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher's capability. KD spans logits transfer, intermediate feature mimicking, relational and attention-based objectives, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and cross-modal variants. Applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which samples or layers to prioritize — KD can produce substantial gains in latency, memory, and sometimes robustness, but it is not a universal remedy: dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher errors are real constraints. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe, summarizes practical patterns that succeed across tasks, highlights empirical failure modes, and gives evidence-backed recommendations for practitioners in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models by transferring information from larger or specialized models. It supports a broad range of objectives beyond raw compression—improving robustness, enabling domain adaptation, supporting privacy-aware or federated workflows, and permitting deployment on constrained hardware. KD methods range from simple soft-label matching to richer transfers of intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational or contrastive structure. While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, alignment between teacher and student, data availability and distribution, and the choice of signals and losses. When applied with attention to these constraints and combined sensibly with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), KD is a practical foundational technique for real-world model compression in vision, language, and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Reese
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Core, Configurable, and Context‑Aware for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with careful teacher–student design, data strategies, and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design—KD routinely yields efficient models that retain much of teacher performance. Its benefits span modalities and deployment settings, but real-world success requires explicit attention to capacity mismatch, data limitations, bias propagation, and distribution shift. Consequently, KD should be the default first-line compression tool but must be applied with task-aware protocols and safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transfer information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Approaches vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or decision-boundary information), by whether original training data are available, and by whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work across vision, multimodal, speech, and natural language tasks shows that careful choices of transfer targets, loss formulations, teacher ensembles, and training schedules can yield compact models that approach — and in some cases match or exceed — teacher performance while enabling deployment under resource, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. Remaining challenges include optimization difficulties that prevent perfect belief matching, distribution-shift and heterogeneity issues in federated or data-free settings, and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Patel
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across modalities KD supports many transfer targets and training protocols and is frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance, but outcomes are context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability and alignment of data all materially affect results. Responsible deployment requires task-aware design, explicit mitigation of failure modes (bias transfer, degraded long-tail performance, distribution shift), and research on robust, data-efficient, and theoretically grounded distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates through multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, synthetic data) and adapts across modalities (vision, speech, graphs, NLP) and deployment constraints (edge inference, federated settings, privacy-aware releases). While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices—teacher quality, what to match, layer alignment, projector usage, data selection, and privacy constraints—and benefits from combining complementary methods such as ensembling, task-adaptive architecture search, and federated or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques constitute a flexible toolkit for transferring behavior and internal structure from large, high‑capacity teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment‑specific student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations, and structured objectives) and across protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co‑distillation, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free, and federated schemes). Empirical practice shows KD often retains a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in compute, memory, and latency when combined with complementary compression methods and careful data and architecture choices. However, KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: it is sensitive to teacher quality and mismatch, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and the risk of propagating teacher artifacts (biases, low‑frequency errors). Remaining needs include principled theory linking distilled signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous or non‑i.i.d. data, and robust privacy/fairness guarantees for compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large, high‑capacity teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative and multimodal tasks, KD has been adapted into many targets and training regimes and is most effective when integrated with architecture‑aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the empirical strengths of KD, the principal methods and protocols, common limitations, and practical design patterns that guide successful compression and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. The literature frames KD as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: common transfer targets include softened logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, and contrastive or adversarial objectives; training regimes span offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher and data-free protocols; and KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-augmentation or synthesis. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains (reduced FLOPs, memory, and latency), but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of signals to transfer, and the availability or generation of appropriate data. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core component of integrated compression pipelines and emphasize safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Lara
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Core for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported family of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. As a practical engineering tool, KD reliably reduces inference cost, memory use, and latency across modalities while often preserving most of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a universal or standalone solution: its effectiveness is conditional on teacher and student design, data regimes, choice of distilled signals, and careful integration with complementary compression primitives and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Treated as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline, KD offers the best balance between efficiency and fidelity for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Integrated Model Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, memory, and latency, but it is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on careful selection of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression primitives and privacy safeguards. Best practice treats KD as the configurable core of an end‑to‑end compression pipeline rather than as a standalone remedy.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. The literature develops multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline multi-stage, online, self-distillation, data-free/generative, adversarial), and application-specific adaptations (NLP transformer compression, vision, speech, graph models, federated and privacy-aware settings). Empirical work shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, data availability, and distributional or fairness concerns. Practical success generally requires matching the distillation objective to the task, handling data limitations with augmentation or synthetic generators, and integrating KD into a broader compression portfolio (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and sometimes improve robustness or task adaptation. A diverse toolkit has been developed—logit/soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and generative data-free techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and selective or meta-learned teaching—and empirical and theoretical work clarifies when and why these choices succeed or fail. Practical deployment requires matching the distilled signal to student capacity and task constraints, handling data- or architecture-mismatch, and explicitly addressing bias and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD has evolved into a diverse toolkit—logit and soft-label transfer, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and data-free or privacy-aware procedures—that when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture replacement) produces compact models suitable for latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployment. Effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and alignment of representations; treating KD as a configurable, task-aware element of a broader compression pipeline yields the most reliable real-world results.

papers_seen.author: Steele
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory use, and communication while preserving task performance. Practitioners apply KD across modalities—vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings—using a variety of targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, curriculum schedules, and data-free/few-shot variants). KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation) and when its design is matched to teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability. Remaining gaps include reliable transfer of robustness and long‑tail behaviors, principled teacher–student co‑design, and data- and privacy-constrained distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central tool to transfer performance from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones across modalities and tasks. The field encompasses diverse mechanisms — from soft-target supervision and feature imitation to contrastive and adversarial schemes — and integrates with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work highlights when and why different formulations help, how to handle limited or absent teacher data, and which practical choices matter for robustness, fairness, and domain-specific demands.

papers_seen.author: Cain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD spans output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocol variants such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, and privacy-aware workflows. In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and must be tailored to teacher/student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; while empirical results across modalities often show students can recover much of teacher performance, important challenges remain in handling capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias and robustness, and formal theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models by transferring information from larger or specialized models. It supports a broad range of objectives beyond raw compression—improving robustness, enabling domain adaptation, supporting privacy-aware or federated workflows, and permitting deployment on constrained hardware. KD methods range from simple soft-label matching to richer transfers of intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational or contrastive structure. While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, alignment between teacher and student, data availability and distribution, and the choice of signals and losses. When applied with attention to these constraints and combined sensibly with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), KD is a practical foundational technique for real-world model compression in vision, language, and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Willis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, multimodal, and structured tasks. The literature frames KD as a configurable toolkit of targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free), and engineering integrations (projectors, curriculum scheduling, data augmentation, architecture search, pruning, quantization). KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve robustness or generalization when applied with task-aware design, but its success is context-dependent: it hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit handling of teacher biases, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Practical systems therefore treat KD as a central component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone, universal recipe.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, multimodal, and graph tasks. When combined with architecture-aware design, layer- and feature-level objectives, adversarial or relational losses, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, NAS), KD enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss and can sometimes improve generalization. KD also faces clear limits—teacher bias, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and optimization instability—that require task-aware curricula, multi-teacher or ensemble strategies, and careful selection of distilled signals. This paper argues that KD should be the first-line instrument in compression toolkits for deep learning and NLP, provided practitioners adopt principled protocols that address known failure modes and integrate KD with complementary methods for the target deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Fleming
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical family of methods for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The literature documents diverse distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), multiple training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free methods), and many integrations with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). Empirical evidence shows KD—when matched to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, and data conditions—can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on careful selection of transfer signals and objectives, appropriate teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including augmentation and synthetic/data‑free approaches), and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, capacity gaps, transferred biases, and distribution shift. Ongoing open problems include formalizing when particular KD signals preserve generalization, distilling reliably under scarce or private data, and principled mitigation of harmful transferred behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The approaches span soft-logit supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and adaptations for special settings such as low-precision inference, multimodal models, graph data, federated learning, and heterogeneous-device training. Empirical work shows KD can improve student accuracy, robustness, and latency while theoretical analyses connect KD to label smoothing and regularization effects. Best practice choices (which teacher signals to match, which samples or augmentations to use, and how to align heterogeneous inputs) materially affect outcomes. This synthesis summarizes known methods, insights about why KD helps, and practical considerations for deploying KD in real-world ML systems.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. The literature frames KD as a flexible, task-aware toolbox: common transfer targets include softened logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, and contrastive or adversarial objectives; training regimes span offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher and data-free protocols; and KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-augmentation or synthesis. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains (reduced FLOPs, memory, and latency), but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of signals to transfer, and the availability or generation of appropriate data. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core component of integrated compression pipelines and emphasize safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Foley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, First‑Line Tool — Powerful but Not Sufficient for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible family of techniques that routinely enables compact, efficient models to inherit much of the behavior and performance of larger teacher models across vision, language, reinforcement learning, and healthcare applications. However, KD is context-sensitive: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity and architecture, the data or synthetic-data strategy used for transfer, and explicit defenses against propagated biases or rare-case failures. The best practical outcomes treat KD as a configurable, task-aware core within an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-level objectives, data strategies (including data-free or adversarial synthesis when needed), and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for producing compact, deployable models from larger teacher models. Across modalities and tasks, KD reduces inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, available data, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Treating KD as a central, configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and safeguards for bias and distributional robustness—yields the most reliable path to deployable, high-performing compressed models.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Bradley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, empirically grounded family of techniques for producing compact student models from large teachers. KD provides a diverse toolbox of targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free and federated variants), and data strategies (augmentation, synthesis, curriculum) that, when selected and tuned to task and deployment constraints, frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. KD is not a plug‑and‑play cure: its practical effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression methods and fairness/robustness safeguards. The following argument synthesizes evidence, limits, and best‑practice recommendations emphasizing KD’s central role within an integrated, context‑aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Klein
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to compact students. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and generative tasks shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and energy cost. KD is not a standalone cure: its practical success depends on choices of distilled signals, teacher–student capacity and architectural alignment, availability or synthesis of data, and careful pairing with complementary compression methods and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Research and engineering priorities include reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, principled selection of distillation targets, mitigation of transferred biases and rare-output degradation, and automated, deployment-aware co-design with pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Alexander
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data strategies—and adopt safeguards for robustness, fairness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick; it is a versatile, practically proven framework that enables resource-efficient deployment, privacy-preserving learning, cross-modal and cross-domain transfers, and even improvements in robustness. When combined with complementary techniques — feature mimicking, projector modules, teacher annealing, label-smoothing–style regularization, and data-free or federated protocols — distillation can address the main bottlenecks of modern deep and multilingual models: size, latency, heterogeneity of devices, limited or private data, and domain shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in any strategy for compressing or adapting deep models for real-world NLP and vision deployments.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. When designed and applied with task awareness—selecting appropriate transfer signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining with complementary compression techniques—KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance under real-world constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student architecture, data availability, and explicit mitigation of risks such as transferred bias, privacy leakage, and degraded handling of rare phenomena. Accordingly, KD is best treated as a configurable core component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a single universal recipe.

papers_seen.author: Salas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from a larger teacher (or ensemble) to a student. Approaches operate at multiple levels—from softened output distributions to intermediate representations, attention or relational maps, and data- or curriculum-aware schedules—and are commonly integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical results across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks show that distillation often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of bias, robustness, and privacy concerns. Ongoing challenges include principled layer-to-layer mappings for heterogeneous architectures, distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, and ensuring transfer of long-tail and robustness properties.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible, empirically validated route to producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods span output-level (soft logits), representation-level (features, attention, relational) and data-aware protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, and data-free). While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and is therefore a natural first-line tool for compression, it is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data regime, and careful handling of robustness, fairness, and privacy. For reliable, production-ready compression, KD should be adopted as a configurable core of an integrated, task- and deployment-aware pipeline that explicitly combines complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and targeted mitigations for known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Santiago
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention and relational signals) and across training regimes (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free and adversarial). Its practical value comes from being a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design and data strategies—rather than a universal, one‑step solution. Realizing KD's benefits requires deliberate teacher–student design, careful handling of data and distributional mismatch, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Warren
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Multifaceted Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a configurable toolkit rather than a single recipe—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to map teacher and student layers, and whether to synthesize or reweight data—KD reliably enables latency-, memory-, and privacy-aware deployment across vision, language, generative, and structured tasks. However, its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, and data availability; therefore best practice combines task-aware distillation objectives with complementary compression techniques and safeguards against transferred errors and biases.

papers_seen.author: Serrano
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal settings, KD methods — from soft‑target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi‑teacher and online schemes, and data‑free or privacy‑aware protocols — consistently improve accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when combined with task‑aware design and complementary compression techniques. Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful attention to teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, what signals are transferred and how layers are mapped, data availability or synthesis strategies, and interventions to mitigate bias, rare‑token degradation, and distribution shift.
