papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Position and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, configurable practical tool for model compression in deep learning and NLP. Empirical syntheses and methodological work show KD reliably produces compact, deployable students from larger teachers across modalities, but its effectiveness is conditional on careful choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data and privacy constraints, and integration with complementary compression methods. Robust, deployable outcomes arise when KD is used as the core element of an integrated pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and explicit safeguards for distributional shift, bias, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: David
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Task‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression (with Explicit Limits and Prescriptions)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs by transferring soft logits and richer internal representations, and it interoperates naturally with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, its success is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and the data strategy strongly determine outcomes. For reliable deployment KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact student models. A wide range of distillation objectives (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive losses), training protocols (offline, online/self-, multi-teacher), and data strategies (full-data, limited-data, data-free, and privacy-aware synthesis) have been proposed and combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical studies show KD often recovers much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and suitable data strategies are available, but KD is context-dependent and must be integrated with task-aware design choices to manage limits related to teacher–student mismatch, optimization, data scarcity, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a diverse set of methods for transferring behavior and representations from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques range from matching soft output distributions to aligning intermediate features, transferring relational structure, adversarial or data‑free supervision, and teacher/student co‑design; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search, KD forms a central part of modern compression pipelines. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently retain much of teacher performance and can improve generalization, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware engineering to address teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve calibration, robustness, or task adaptation. The field has evolved from logits-based soft-target training to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free approaches, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, handling limited or mismatched data, and explicitly addressing risks such as transferred biases or privacy leakage. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a single turnkey algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Goodman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal structure from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods include output-level soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online/self- and multi-teacher protocols, and data‑free or privacy-aware synthesis. When combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design, KD routinely produces substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter footprint while retaining much of teacher performance. The effectiveness of KD is highly context dependent: it relies on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis strategies, and explicit treatment of robustness, fairness, and privacy. Remaining challenges include principled teacher–student design, reliable distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, mitigation of bias transfer, and automation of distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Craig
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. Across modalities and tasks, a diverse toolbox of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed and combined with complementary compression methods to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical results show that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable practical deployment, but success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and explicit measures to mitigate failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization gaps, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Davies
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesized Evidence and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically driven set of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A rich design space has emerged—output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data‑free or privacy-aware synthesis—together with pipelines that combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical work shows that when teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, and distillation data are carefully managed, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute. Practical deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align layers and inputs, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate the propagation of teacher errors, bias, and degradation on low-frequency behaviors; combining KD with complementary compression techniques and tailored curricula typically yields the best accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When adapted to task, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD preserves much of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprint, and improved adaptability across domains and modalities. However, KD is a family of techniques rather than a single algorithm: best outcomes arise from combining distillation with complementary methods (e.g., pruning, architecture search, curriculum design, data synthesis) and from explicitly addressing challenges such as imperfect teachers, domain shift, privacy, and heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Austin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate over multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure) and training protocols (offline, online/self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical work across vision, language, multimodal, and retrieval tasks shows KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute. Reliable application treats KD as a configurable, task‑aware component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with data strategies, architecture alignment, and complementary primitives such as pruning and quantization—and requires explicit validation for robustness, fairness, privacy, and rare‑case behavior.

papers_seen.author: Drake
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation protocols, and data-aware or data-free approaches. When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD frequently enables large reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. However, successful application is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer signals, and data availability (or synthesis) strongly influence outcomes. Robust deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines that explicitly address distribution shift, long-tail behavior, bias transfer, and privacy or device constraints.

papers_seen.author: Garrett
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically oriented family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Modern KD extends well beyond soft-target/logit matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free or adversarial synthesis, and multi-teacher or online training regimes. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline — aligned to teacher and student architectures, data availability, and deployment constraints — and combined with complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Important practical limits remain (teacher–student capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or bias, domain shift, and scarce or private data), motivating task-aware design choices, layer-mapping strategies, and privacy-preserving or data-synthesis approaches.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework that reliably produces compact, deployable models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and relational objectives—have been shown across vision, language, recommendation, and generative tasks to reduce latency and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is not a singular cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data choices, and objective design, and it can propagate biases or fail on rare or out-of-distribution phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline, combined with architecture-aware mapping, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and targeted safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Weiss
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical, flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. The literature shows a broad family of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations), multiple training paradigms (offline, online, co-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and frequent combination with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD works both as a method for transferring predictive behavior and as an implicit regularizer, but its empirical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability (including synthesized or data‑free regimes), and careful engineering choices to mitigate optimization gaps, distributional mismatch, and transferred biases.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and powerful technique for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When matched to the task and deployment constraints, KD can preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs; its value increases when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware design. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, data and curriculum strategies, teacher–student compatibility, and mitigation of transferred biases and rare-case failures. Treating KD as a configurable, first-order element of an integrated compression pipeline—rather than a one-shot solution—yields the best tradeoffs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Parks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Sensitive Tool Best Used in an Integrated Compression Portfolio
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an adaptable and empirically validated family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD alone is rarely sufficient for production-grade compression: capacity mismatch, limited or private data, teacher errors and biases, and robustness concerns limit off‑the‑shelf success. The strongest practical outcomes arise when KD is embedded in a hybrid pipeline that combines representation-level matching, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — A Position and Recommended Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows that KD can reduce inference cost, latency, and memory requirements and enable deployment under privacy, communication, and resource constraints. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, unbiased, or optimal compressed models: failures arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, transfer of teacher errors and biases, poor handling of low-frequency phenomena, and vulnerability under distribution shift or adversarial attack. Practical compression therefore treats KD as a core component within an integrated pipeline—combining representation-aware objectives, curriculum and sample-selection strategies, adversarial or synthetic-data generation for data-scarce regimes, and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to realize reliable, resource-aware students.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile paradigm for producing smaller, deployable models by transferring informative behavior from larger teacher models into compact students. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants and protocols enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: reliable deployment requires task‑aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student co‑design, data and privacy strategies, and complementary compression techniques. I argue KD should be treated as the default, configurable core of integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from large teachers across vision, language, graph, and generative settings. KD supports deployment on constrained hardware, domain adaptation, improved interpretability, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Ballard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to produce deployable systems under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of KD objectives and training regimes—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate feature and relation-level imitation, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) enables substantial efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD�s practical success is conditional on task-aware choices about what to transfer, teacher�student alignment, data availability and augmentation, and explicit handling of bias, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a broadly applicable paradigm that enables deployment of large models across modalities, supports privacy- and resource-constrained federated scenarios, and improves generalization when combined with task- and architecture-specific techniques. Empirical evidence shows that KD alone yields large gains for small students, while hybrid approaches that distill internal representations, use curriculum or meta-learning, augment data, or jointly optimize architecture and distillation produce state-of-the-art trade-offs between size, speed, and task performance. KD is therefore a foundational tool for modern model compression strategies and should be used in concert with complementary methods (e.g., pretraining, low-precision numerics, structural compression, and privacy-aware distillation) to meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Becker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teacher models. When designed and applied with attention to what signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data and complementary compression primitives are used, KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success is bounded by teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis, and risks such as bias transfer and degraded behavior on rare or out‑of‑distribution phenomena. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable core of integrated compression pipelines rather than a stand‑alone solution.

papers_seen.author: Hester
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically proven family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely improves efficiency (latency, memory, compute) while often recovering a large fraction of teacher performance, but its success is conditional: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, distilled signals, data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes determine outcomes. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline (pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and robustness/privacy safeguards) rather than a turn‑key cure.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels — soft targets (logits), intermediate representations, attention and relational structure, and contrastive objectives — and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, pretraining, and architecture adaptation. Practical success is conditional on teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful optimization and evaluation to avoid propagating teacher artifacts, degrading rare-case behavior, or failing under distribution shift. The field shows strong empirical gains across vision, language, speech, recommendation, generative, and multimodal tasks, while open problems remain in theory, heterogeneous architectures, privacy-aware protocols, and robust transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Kelly
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teachers into smaller students. When treated as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines and paired with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthesis, privacy-preserving protocols), KD routinely yields large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. Its success is, however, conditional: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigation of propagated biases, rare-case failures, and distribution shift determine outcomes. Best practice treats KD not as a turnkey cure but as a task‑aware, engineered component of end-to-end compression and evaluation workflows.

papers_seen.author: Weber
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocols such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free or privacy-aware variants. Distillation is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data strategies; its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and loss of rare behaviors. Remaining research directions include principled theory linking distillation objectives to generalization, reliable distillation under data scarcity and heterogeneous architectures, and methods that preserve robustness, fairness, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Levy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central but Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, widely adopted family of techniques for producing smaller, deployable models from larger teachers across deep learning and NLP. KD reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves much of teacher performance, but its success is strongly context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regime, and the choice of distilled signals determine outcomes. For robust, production-ready compression, KD should be treated as the configurable core of an integrated pipeline combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), task-aware design, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Cain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD spans output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocol variants such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, and privacy-aware workflows. In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and must be tailored to teacher/student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; while empirical results across modalities often show students can recover much of teacher performance, important challenges remain in handling capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias and robustness, and formal theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Rowe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. While KD often preserves much of teacher performance, its success is context dependent and requires careful choices about distillation targets, teacher–student alignment, and data handling; open problems remain in principled target selection, robustness to distribution shift and rare outputs, and automated teacher–student matching.

papers_seen.author: Lopez

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. The literature develops multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline multi-stage, online, self-distillation, data-free/generative, adversarial), and application-specific adaptations (NLP transformer compression, vision, speech, graph models, federated and privacy-aware settings). Empirical work shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, data availability, and distributional or fairness concerns. Practical success generally requires matching the distillation objective to the task, handling data limitations with augmentation or synthetic generators, and integrating KD into a broader compression portfolio (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Byrd

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. papers_seen.author: Cox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, configurable family of methods for producing compact, efficient models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models. KD methods span output-level supervision, intermediate representation and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocols such as offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free regimes. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and generative tasks shows KD routinely enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while recovering much of teacher performance when integrated into task‑aware compression pipelines that include pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Important practical limits—teacher–student capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, distribution shift, and data scarcity or privacy constraints—motivate careful objective selection, data strategies (including synthesis and privacy‑aware approaches), and explicit evaluation before deployment.

papers_seen.author: Roach
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods span output-level supervision (soft logits), intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive losses, adversarial and data-free generation, online and multi-teacher protocols, and self-distillation. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks shows KD frequently yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are carefully matched. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline alongside pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and calls for explicit strategies to mitigate teacher bias, handle data scarcity or privacy constraints, and maintain rare-token or long-tail behaviors. Remaining challenges include principled signal selection for heterogeneous architectures, robust and private distillation under non‑i.i.d. data, and automated, deployment‑aware teacher–student co‑design.

papers_seen.author: Stein
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used family of techniques for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller students to reduce latency, memory, and energy costs while preserving task performance. Across vision, language, and multimodal domains, KD has evolved beyond logits-only supervision into rich protocols that match intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized data or generator-based replay. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and careful objective and layer alignment. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, practical recommendations, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Duarte
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (logits, features, relations) and in varied data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free), and they are most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task-aware choices about what to transfer. While KD often preserves much of teacher performance, its success is context-dependent: it relies on teacher quality, student capacity, suitable data or synthetic-data protocols, and explicit strategies to protect rare outputs and fairness under distribution shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution, and I provide actionable guidance and open problems to prioritize in research and practice.

papers_seen.author: Bates
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, and privacy. KD methods range from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature, attention/relational, and contrastive objectives, and they operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, and data-constrained regimes. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when designed with attention to teacher–student compatibility and data strategy, KD routinely produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance. However, KD is context-dependent: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals and data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and distribution shift. Ongoing challenges include principled theory linking objectives to guarantees, robust and private distillation under heterogeneous or limited data, and automated, task-aware design of KD within integrated compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically proven family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD spans outputs-only approaches (soft targets) to rich objectives that match intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, or contrastive signals. It operates across many data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free, synthetic-data), and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to achieve deployment constraints on latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity. The effectiveness of KD is strongly context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies (including augmentation, curriculum, and synthetic generation). Common failure modes include propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors, and optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, motivating targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Vance
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component: The Case for Integrated, Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applied method for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller students. However, KD faces concrete limitations—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity or privacy constraints, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and potential fairness or robustness regressions—that reduce its effectiveness when used alone. The strongest practical outcomes come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful selection or synthesis of distilled supervision, and task- and data-aware training schedules.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Insufficient Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a broad family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models so they can be deployed under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. The KD toolkit includes logits/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free schemes, online and self-distillation, and multi-teacher workflows; in practice KD is typically combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and stabilizes student training, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, distillation targets and data availability, and task-specific factors (e.g., classification vs. generation). Progress comes from treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component of integrated compression pipelines and from innovations in feature-based objectives, adversarial and curriculum strategies, data synthesis, and privacy-aware formulations.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students to meet constraints of latency, memory, compute, or privacy. However, KD is context dependent: its success hinges on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and mitigation of failure modes. As a result, KD should be treated as the central, configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone, sufficient solution.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from large, expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, efficient models. Methods include logit-based distillation, feature- or representation-based matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving approaches, and combinations with pruning or architecture search. KD has been applied across modalities and domains—vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, generative models, and healthcare—demonstrating gains in inference efficiency, robustness, generalization, and interpretability when appropriately designed. Open challenges remain around data availability, teacher–student mismatch, selection of distilled signals and samples, and principled integration with other compression techniques; recent work proposes meta-learning teachers, adaptive teacher weighting, projector modules, and task-adaptive compression as practical remedies.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, evidence-backed approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable models across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD methods — ranging from logits transfer to intermediate-feature matching, self-distillation, and selective-sample protocols — routinely enable substantial reductions in compute, memory, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. When treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline, KD provides a practical route to deploy high-performing models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

When combined with complementary compression techniques and careful training protocols, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and domain constraints; however, its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, the choice of distilled signals, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation and degraded modeling of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Crawford
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Versatile, and Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used family of techniques for transferring the behavior and internal representations of large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive objectives, and data-free or self-distillation protocols—frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and careful choice of objectives and pipeline design. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression strategy that combines representation-aware distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping, and targeted measures to mitigate bias, rare-token degradation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students. It reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment across modalities when paired with careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or mismatched data. KD should be treated as a core, necessary element of practical compression pipelines but not as a standalone solution: the best results come from integrating KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from applying context-aware design and mitigation for bias, robustness, and data constraints.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely adopted approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, data strategies, and privacy- or domain-aware adaptations—rather than a universal, standalone cure-all. I argue KD should be the default core of model-compression workflows while being explicitly adapted to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical family of methods for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The literature documents diverse distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), multiple training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free methods), and many integrations with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). Empirical evidence shows KD—when matched to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, and data conditions—can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on careful selection of transfer signals and objectives, appropriate teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including augmentation and synthetic/data‑free approaches), and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, capacity gaps, transferred biases, and distribution shift. Ongoing open problems include formalizing when particular KD signals preserve generalization, distilling reliably under scarce or private data, and principled mitigation of harmful transferred behaviors.

Reliable deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—aligned to teacher and student architectures, data availability, and deployment constraints—and combines distillation with complementary techniques and targeted safeguards to mitigate teacher error, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial or data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—have been shown to recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful selection of what and how to transfer; open challenges remain in robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and enabling private or data-free distillation at scale.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models so the students meet latency, memory, compute, or privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. KD variants operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals) and across diverse data regimes (full-data, limited-data, and data-free). Empirical evidence shows KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when integrated into end-to-end compression pipelines that also use pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies. Practical deployment requires task- and capacity-aware design, careful teacher–student co‑design, and explicit safeguards for failure modes such as propagated bias, degraded low‑frequency behavior, and distribution shift; these remain active areas for research.

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative settings. KD reliably improves student performance when teacher quality, the form of transferred signals, and data/augmentation strategies are chosen to match the task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not sufficient by itself: best outcomes arise when distillation is integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful data or augmentation strategies, and task- or architecture-aware adaptations. This article argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure-all, and it highlights empirical evidence, mechanisms, limitations, and practical recommendations drawn from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible approach to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, distillation can recover accuracy for lightweight architectures, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and transfer specialized properties (e.g., temporal, structural, or ensemble knowledge). However, distillation is not a panacea: its success depends on the choice of teacher, student architecture and capacity, the training protocol (including data augmentation and sample selection), and implementation details that affect optimization. When these factors are treated carefully, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, architecture design, quantization) and can be adapted to domain-specific needs such as federated learning, retrieval, and vision-language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, pragmatic set of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can preserve much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD is effective across modalities and tasks when its objectives, training protocols, and data strategies are chosen to match the task, teacher–student capacities, and deployment constraints; however, KD has clear failure modes and limits that require integrated mitigation. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of end-to-end compression pipelines rather than a standalone, one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable, and Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. KD routinely yields compact, deployable models that recover much of teacher performance when it is applied as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness. Real-world success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of known failure modes such as bias propagation and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD encompasses a diverse set of transfer targets and protocols and is routinely combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture design). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD can preserve a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but its effectiveness is context dependent: success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards against propagated biases, privacy leakage, and degraded behavior on low-frequency or out-of-distribution phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a broadly applicable paradigm that enables deployment of large models across modalities, supports privacy- and resource-constrained federated scenarios, and improves generalization when combined with task- and architecture-specific techniques. Empirical evidence shows that KD alone yields large gains for small students, while hybrid approaches that distill internal representations, use curriculum or meta-learning, augment data, or jointly optimize architecture and distillation produce state-of-the-art trade-offs between size, speed, and task performance. KD is therefore a foundational tool for modern model compression strategies and should be used in concert with complementary methods (e.g., pretraining, low-precision numerics, structural compression, and privacy-aware distillation) to meet real-world deployment constraints.
