papers_seen.author: Cordova
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely reduces inference cost and memory while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its reliability is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, architecture alignment, and complementary compression primitives critically shape outcomes. A pragmatic recommendation is to treat KD as the central component of compression pipelines while explicitly adapting objectives, data protocols, and auxiliary methods to the deployment constraints and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployment-ready students while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation techniques include matching logits (soft labels), feature- and layer-level imitation, ensemble and online schemes, data-free approaches, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Practical success depends on teacher quality and design, how and what information is transferred, availability and nature of data used for distillation, and how distillation is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications span NLP (BERT compression, reading comprehension, language generation), vision and generative models (GANs, lipreading, 3D detection), recommender systems, and graphs. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher-student architectures, preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, preventing transfer of teacher biases, and robust distillation under distribution shift or limited data.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible method for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence shows KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance, but its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distillation signals, data availability or synthesis, and complementary compression techniques. For robust, fair, and hardware‑aware deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable, context‑aware core within integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment and domain-specific use. Across modalities and tasks, KD can preserve much of the teacher's performance in compact students, but it must be combined with task-aware engineering—such as teacher adaptation, layer-wise selection, data augmentation, and hardware-aware pruning—to address heterogeneity, domain shift, and efficiency constraints. This article argues that KD is necessary but not sufficient: best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques chosen for the target modality, deployment constraints, and learning scenario.

papers_seen.author: Khan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Core for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques that enables compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teachers to smaller students. KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, and has been adapted to many objectives, training protocols, and modalities. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal compression; reliable deployment treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes teacher–student co‑design, data strategies, and complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Addressing remaining challenges — theoretical understanding, low‑data and heterogeneous regimes, privacy, and long‑tail behavior — requires targeted research and practical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Cisneros
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods transfer information at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention and relational structure) and succeed across modalities when integrated into task‑aware compression pipelines. While KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, reliable deployment requires explicit attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and safeguards against bias and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A large family of distillation objectives and training protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free schemes, and online or multi-teacher setups—and these are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while lowering latency and memory, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Open problems include robust and private distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mapping for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and deployment‑specialized models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Methods include matching soft logits, aligning intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and online protocols, and data‑aware or data‑free variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable tool within an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation, rare‑token degradation, and distribution shift. Practical deployments therefore combine careful selection of transfer targets, layer and projector design, curricula and data synthesis, and complementary compression primitives while monitoring robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Hines
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across modalities when the distilled signals, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen carefully, but its effectiveness is context dependent and improved when incorporated into an integrated compression pipeline with complementary methods and safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative modeling, researchers transfer information via softened output distributions, intermediate-feature matching, relational and attention maps, and many-to-many layer alignment. Variants address resource heterogeneity, data unavailability, privacy, robustness, and fairness. Empirical and analytic work shows that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, but its success depends on design choices (what to transfer, teacher quality, data or pseudo-data, and alignment losses). State-of-the-art practice mixes logits-based loss with feature- or representation-level objectives, task-aware augmentations, and architecture- or training-aware modifications to obtain favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs in deployment.

papers_seen.author: Beard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance and functionality of larger teacher models. KD is highly versatile—operating at the level of logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational objectives—and is effective across modalities (vision, language, speech, recommender systems, and generative models). However, its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and distribution, and the design of distillation objectives; consequently KD should be treated as a configurable component that is combined with complementary compression techniques and deployment-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students that preserves much of teacher functionality while reducing latency, memory, and compute. KD methods span soft-logit matching, intermediate-representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD delivers substantial practical benefits across modalities and tasks when applied as part of a task-aware compression pipeline, but it is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching
papers_seen.abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core with Clear Limits — Guidance for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely useful set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher's capability. KD spans logits transfer, intermediate feature mimicking, relational and attention-based objectives, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and cross-modal variants. Applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which samples or layers to prioritize — KD can produce substantial gains in latency, memory, and sometimes robustness, but it is not a universal remedy: dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher errors are real constraints. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe, summarizes practical patterns that succeed across tasks, highlights empirical failure modes, and gives evidence-backed recommendations for practitioners in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD transfers information from teacher to student via soft logits, intermediate representations, attentional or channel signals, and relational objectives; it is often combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain-adaptation constraints. While KD frequently preserves much of a teacher’s performance and can improve robustness or generalization in some settings, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and responsible handling of bias, privacy, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Uses, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical deployments use KD as one component in an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—and require task‑aware choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Known limitations include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, degraded performance on long‑tail or rare outputs, and sensitivity to distribution shift; these motivate multi‑teacher, selective, or data‑synthesis protocols and careful evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Webb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Tool, Context-Aware Integration
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. KD variants—matching logits, imitating intermediate representations or attention, using multi-teacher or self-distillation regimes, and supporting data-free or privacy-aware setups—have demonstrated broad applicability across vision, speech, language, retrieval, and multimodal tasks. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and fidelity of distillation data, and task-specific needs. Best outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful layer and feature alignment, and data- or task-aware strategies to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Versatile Toolkit with Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. Across NLP and vision applications, KD enables deployment on resource-constrained hardware, supports privacy- and data-constrained settings, and can be adapted to preserve or transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, cross-modal behavior, and domain expertise. At the same time, KD interacts with factors such as teacher quality, data availability, label design, and training cost, and several specialized methods have been developed to address these practical trade-offs. This paper argues that KD is an indispensable, flexible approach for model compression and adaptation, and that best results arise from combining KD with complementary practices (e.g., pre-training, augmentation, curriculum selection, or generative replay) tailored to the deployment constraints and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Bentley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multifaceted Toolbox for Compression and Responsible Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as a versatile, task- and domain-adaptive toolbox rather than a single recipe. When combined with complementary mechanisms (feature and layer matching, many-to-many alignment, data augmentation, ensembling, pruning, quantization, and privacy-preserving protocols), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving—or in some cases improving—task performance. Realizing these benefits reliably requires attention to what is distilled, how teacher and student are matched, and measures to mitigate risks such as teacher bias, data scarcity, and privacy concerns. Practical adoption should therefore treat KD as a configurable component of compression and deployment pipelines, with choices driven by the task, data availability, and safety constraints.

papers_seen.author: Willis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, multimodal, and structured tasks. The literature frames KD as a configurable toolkit of targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free), and engineering integrations (projectors, curriculum scheduling, data augmentation, architecture search, pruning, quantization). KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve robustness or generalization when applied with task-aware design, but its success is context-dependent: it hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit handling of teacher biases, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Practical systems therefore treat KD as a central component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone, universal recipe.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. A broad set of methods—logit-level transfer, feature- and relation-level matching, adversarial and data-free protocols, and task-aware adaptations—enables KD to serve as a first-order component of practical compression pipelines. However, its success is conditional on teacher–student design, data regime, what is distilled, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD operates at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structures—and is effective across modalities (vision, language, speech, and translation) when adapted to task constraints. KD achieves substantial reductions in latency and model size while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate transferred biases and low-frequency or out-of-distribution failures. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, central component of an integrated compression and deployment pipeline rather than as a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. A rich family of KD formulations — from logit matching and feature imitation to adversarial, data-free, and online schemes — together with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and teacher ensembles) enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while largely preserving model quality. However, KD is not universally effective out-of-the-box: its benefits and risks depend on task characteristics, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and deliberate choices of what and how to transfer. When practitioners treat KD as a toolkit of targeted strategies and validate choices against task constraints, it yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to the original model.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Responsible NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into efficient students while also serving as a lever for regularization, robustness, privacy, fairness, interpretability, and continual/multi-task learning. When applied thoughtfully—combining soft-label distillation with feature- and representation-level matching, layer mapping, attention or projector modules, and task-aware curricula—KD can produce lightweight models that approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance on constrained devices and specialized tasks. However, KD is not automatic: optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and mismatches in the information transferred (e.g., for low-frequency tokens or internal features) limit its effectiveness unless complemented by targeted methodological choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe: choose distillation targets (outputs, features, internal representations), mapping strategies (many-to-many layer mapping, attention, projectors), and auxiliary safeguards (privacy-preserving noise, fairness interventions, adversarial distillation) to align compression goals with safety and utility requirements.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students. KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation- and relation-based objectives, layer mapping, online/ensemble schemes, and data-synthesis methods—have been applied across vision, NLP, translation, retrieval, federated learning, and privacy-sensitive releases. When designed with task-awareness (selecting what to distill, aligning teacher and student, and engineering the distillation data and objectives) and combined with complementary compression tools, KD often yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and potential transfer of teacher errors or biases require careful mitigation. Best practice is to treat KD as a first-class element of a compression toolbox—default to distillation but tailor its form to task and deployment constraints, and combine it with architectural, data, and privacy-aware procedures to achieve robust, deployable models.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Hayes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — An Argument for Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely adopted approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. Empirical evidence across modalities shows KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, memory, and latency. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of transferred signals, and availability or synthesis of appropriate data. For robust, fair, and production-ready compression, KD should operate as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that combine representation matching, data strategies, and architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or layer adaptation).

papers_seen.author: Stephens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD routinely produces compact models that retain a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success is strongly context dependent: it requires task‑aware design of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and explicit mitigations for known failure modes. The practical position argued here is that KD should be treated as the configurable, central element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis/augmentation, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: French
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Across modalities and tasks, a broad set of distillation targets and protocols—ranging from soft logits to intermediate feature and attention matching, relational or contrastive signals, and data‑free synthesis—has enabled substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance. Effectiveness is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and careful design of objectives, layer alignment, and complementary compression steps determine outcomes. Open problems include principled theory of transfer, robust transfer under distribution shift or privacy constraints, and preserving rare or structured outputs in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Findings from the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. The literature treats KD as a flexible, configurable component of compression pipelines rather than a single recipe: methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel- or relation-level signals), how transfer is organized (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free/zero-shot), and how KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). Empirical evidence shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the chosen distillation signals and objectives, and data availability or synthesis strategies. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable, task-aware tool integrated with other compression and robustness practices.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods (logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data- or generator-based synthesis) and training regimes (offline, online, self-, and multi-teacher) are routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, available data or synthesis strategies, and mitigation of failure modes such as propagated teacher bias, optimization and capacity mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student co-design, and targeted safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a diverse set of methods for transferring behavior and representations from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques range from matching soft output distributions to aligning intermediate features, transferring relational structure, adversarial or data‑free supervision, and teacher/student co‑design; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search, KD forms a central part of modern compression pipelines. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently retain much of teacher performance and can improve generalization, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware engineering to address teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: The Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression (but Not a Standalone Cure)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable technique for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, and data-free variants), and combinations with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, detection, and healthcare shows KD routinely enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and careful objective and architecture design. Best practice treats KD as the central, configurable element of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that explicitly addresses data scarcity, distribution shift, privacy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Conditional Component of Hybrid Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports deployment under compute, latency, and privacy constraints, its reliability depends on task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and complementary compression methods. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable core within hybrid compression pipelines, paired with complementary techniques and explicit safeguards to address robustness, fairness, and data- or privacy-limited settings.

papers_seen.author: Hart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior and performance of larger teachers. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when integrated thoughtfully into compression pipelines and paired with complementary techniques, but its effectiveness is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student design, data strategy, and safeguards for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining much of the teacher’s performance. The literature shows a diverse toolkit of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure, channel statistics, and contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free variants), and task-aware adaptations (layer mapping, projector modules, synthetic-data generation, and curriculum/annealing). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, multimodal tasks, and continual or federated settings demonstrates substantial efficiency gains but also highlights persistent challenges: teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatch, limited or unavailable training data, propagation of teacher biases or errors, distribution shift, and difficulties transferring rare or low-frequency behaviors. Practical success typically requires matching the distillation signal to task and student capacity and integrating KD with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: A Central but Context‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practically effective set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, distillation yields substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often recovering much of teacher performance. However, its success is highly context dependent: outcomes hinge on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and training protocol, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. For robust, fair, and production-ready compression, distillation should be deployed as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that combine architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, privacy, and long‑tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for producing compact models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants and complementary compression methods enable substantial reductions in computation, memory, and latency while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and integration with other compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Salinas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, diverse family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large or composite teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. The field has evolved from matching soft output probabilities to include feature- and layer-level imitation, attention and relational transfer, contrastive and adversarial objectives, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols, and online or multi-teacher schemes. KD is effective across modalities and tasks (vision, NLP, speech, graphs, and multimodal systems) and often forms part of a broader compression pipeline together with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD success depends on task-aware choices—teacher quality, student capacity, the distillation signal, and the data available—and several practical challenges remain, including distribution shift, data heterogeneity (especially in federated settings), low-frequency/rare-token behavior, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Configurable Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals), diverse scheduling regimes (offline, online, progressive), and synergistic combination with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest loss in task performance, its success is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability (or synthetic/data-free strategies), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, robustness, and privacy concerns determine outcomes. Consequently, KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable tool in compression pipelines—selected and tuned according to task, data, and deployment constraints—rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression: Efficacy, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD encompasses a range of transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structures), training protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation), and deployment strategies (data‑constrained, privacy‑aware, federated and heterogeneous devices). While KD is an effective first‑line tool for many compression needs, its success depends on careful choice of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Responsible deployment requires explicit safeguards against propagating teacher errors, biased behavior, and degradation on low‑frequency or out‑of‑distribution phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to meet deployment constraints such as latency, memory, compute, and privacy. Across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains, KD spans soft‑target/logit matching, intermediate‑feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocols including offline, online/self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free distillation. Empirical work shows KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs and can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data regimes, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). However, KD’s effectiveness is context‑dependent: reliable deployment requires teacher–student co‑design, careful choice of distilled signals, appropriate data strategies, and mitigations for failure modes such as capacity mismatch, transferred biases, distribution shift, and degradation on rare/low‑frequency phenomena. Important open problems include principled objectives, robust/private distillation under data scarcity, and distillation for heterogeneous or structured/generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, often more expressive teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Methods vary in what is transferred (teacher logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure), how training is scheduled (offline, online, self-distillation, multi‑teacher, curricula), and whether original training data are used or synthesized. KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and when its design is matched to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. Common practical concerns include capacity and optimization mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and reliable transfer of robustness and long‑tail behavior; addressing these requires task‑aware signal selection, layer‑mapping strategies, data synthesis or privacy‑aware protocols, and explicit evaluation of robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Randall
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted approach for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. A broad family of distillation objectives and protocols — including soft-logit matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and contrastive signals, multi-/self-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data workflows, and privacy-aware variants — has been shown to recover much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks when applied as a task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline. Practical success depends on careful choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and curation of distillation data (or effective synthetic alternatives), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as bias propagation, capacity mismatch, degraded long-tail or low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Combining KD with complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied engineering (layer mapping, projectors, curriculum or annealing) yields the most reliable real-world results, while open challenges remain around theory, data-efficient protocols, privacy guarantees, and preserving rare-case behaviors.

papers_seen.author: York
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Conditional Component of Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and reduces inference latency, memory, and energy, but its effectiveness is context-dependent. For robust, production-grade compression, KD should be treated as the default core of integrated, task- and deployment-aware compression pipelines that combine careful teacher–student co‑design, signal selection, data strategies (including synthesis and privacy-aware protocols), and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Important open work remains on principled theory of transferable signals, privacy- and fairness-aware distillation, and reliable distillation across heterogeneous architectures and structured/generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential component of modern model-compression pipelines: it enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a universal remedy. KD’s strengths arise from flexible transfer targets (logits, features, attention, relational signals), multiple training paradigms (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and natural compatibility with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Real-world success requires task‑ and capacity‑aware choices, data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or privacy-aware data), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as teacher bias transfer, teacher–student mismatch, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Treated as a configurable, task‑conditional component within an integrated compression pipeline, KD is the practical backbone of deployable deep and NLP models.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Jenkins
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and deployment constraints. KD methods include matching soft logits, aligning intermediate features and attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online/self-distillation protocols, and data‑free or synthetic-data variants. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs and generative settings shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in inference cost; however, benefits are strongly context dependent on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable element inside integrated compression pipelines and emphasize targeted evaluation of robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, multimodal, and generative domains show KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Practical deployment favors combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), choosing appropriate transfer targets (logits, features, attention, decision-boundary signals), and adopting data- and task-aware strategies. KD also has well-documented limitations — optimization obstacles that prevent perfect teacher matching, sensitivity to teacher quality and data regimes, and risks of propagating teacher biases or poor modeling of rare phenomena — which motivate targeted mitigations such as adversarial/sample-selection methods, multi-teacher and teacher-aware schemes, data-free or privacy-preserving formulations, and representation-level objectives. Overall, KD is best viewed as a flexible, task-aware toolkit whose effectiveness depends on matching methods and safeguards to the compression and deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from large teachers across vision, language, graph, and generative settings. KD supports deployment on constrained hardware, domain adaptation, improved interpretability, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, graph, and generative settings, KD techniques (logits, feature/attention matching, relational objectives, adversarial and data‑free protocols, and ensemble/online schemes) often recover a large fraction of teacher performance when paired with appropriate data strategies, pretraining, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD has concrete limits — teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, rare‑token degradation, and failures under distribution shift or scarce/private data — which motivate task‑aware design, multi‑signal objectives, and integration with other compression primitives. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, domain examples, practical guidelines, and open challenges documented in the selected literature.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Campbell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Context‑Aware, and Best Used Within Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models. KD reduces inference cost and memory footprint and enables deployment in latency-, compute-, and privacy-constrained environments. Its many variants—logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi-/self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—have shown broad empirical success across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. Despite this success, KD’s effectiveness is strongly context-dependent: it requires careful attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and fidelity, and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, degraded rare-case behavior, and fairness or privacy concerns. Treating KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline (combining pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies) yields the most reliable results for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD operates via many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, adversarial or data‑free generation, and online or multi‑teacher training—and is typically combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet practical latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware design, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful engineering to avoid failure modes such as teacher error transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Potts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Tool Best Used in Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD consistently improves accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when adapted to task and deployment constraints, but it is not a standalone solution: reliable compression requires attention to what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Practical use of KD therefore treats it as a configurable core of a broader, context‑aware model‑compression pipeline.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring outputs, internal representations, or relational structure. A broad empirical literature shows KD yields strong efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs across vision, language, and multimodal tasks when integrated with complementary compression techniques and task-aware engineering. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regimes, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias propagation and distribution shift.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, choice of distilled signals, and data availability. Best results arise when KD is treated as a configurable toolkit integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful layer- and task-alignment, and safeguards for bias, privacy, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Shah
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically essential family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. KD supports multiple transfer targets and training protocols, is routinely combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and has been applied across modalities (language, vision, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks). Its empirical success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and careful design of what and how to transfer; persistent challenges include robustness, privacy, and reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models or ensembles into smaller, deployable student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while retaining much of task performance. Modern KD methods span soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence indicates KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and suitable data strategies are aligned, but its success is context-dependent and requires task-aware design to mitigate limits related to teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Jimenez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Insufficient — Positioning KD as the Core of Integrated Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when its objectives, the information transferred, and data strategies are chosen to fit the student architecture and deployment context. At the same time, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit interventions for robustness, fairness, and low-frequency behavior. Treating KD as a configurable core inside a broader compression pipeline—combined deliberately with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and task-aware data strategies—offers the most reliable path to deployable, efficient, and responsible models.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers capabilities of large models into smaller ones via indirect supervision. Methods vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and practical constraints (limited data, privacy, cross-distribution generalization, modality mismatch). Empirical work across speech, vision, language, retrieval, graph, generative modeling, and medical imaging shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while gaining resource efficiency; theoretical analyses and diagnostic studies clarify mechanisms and guide designs such as projector layers, many-to-many layer mapping, and curriculum or data-augmentation strategies. Remaining challenges include distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, robust transfer of inductive biases, and principled layer-to-layer alignment for heterogeneous architectures.

Across vision, language, speech, and graph tasks, KD uses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline multi‑teacher, online/self‑distillation, data‑free or generator‑based synthesis, and federated/zero‑shot transfer). KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search or NAS) and when adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints. However, practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, low‑frequency failures, and distribution shift. Treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—choosing appropriate signals, layer mappings, data strategies, and complementary techniques—yields the most reliable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.
